Multiple road closures were reported due to downed trees and powerlines across roadways.  Measured gusts ranged from 40-54 mph between 2 am on 8/5 through 7 am on 8/5. Wind damage started to impact the county during the evening of 8/4. At 8 pm local time, a tree was blown down near NW 43rd Street in Gainesville. By 9:13 pm local time, all lines of State Road 24 in Gainesville had to be closed due to a downed tree. Fallen trees were also reported blocking all lanes along SR-222. Fallen trees and downed power lines were also reported across the University of Florida campus. In Gainesville and Alachua, a number of homes suffered minor to major damage due to flooding, and several trees fell onto homes. On 8/5 at 8:11 am EDT, State Warning Point relayed a report that there was damage to a residence in Alachua due to a tree of unknown size that destroyed the home, but with no injuries.  About 8.75 inches of rainfall was measured by a CoCoRaHS observer at Brooker 1.6 SW during Debby. On the University of Florida campus, the EM relayed that there were several trees blown down, minor roadway flooding at times and water flooded into a few buildings. The WeatherStem on campus measured 7.19 inches of storm total rainfall and the highest wind gust was 54 mph during the early morning hours of 8/5. At the Santa Fe Community College in Gainesville, the EM reported significant water damage was reported at several campus buildings and downed tree limbs and wires were blown down.

Several inches of water was reported across Southern States Nursery Rd in Macclenny. The St. Marys River near Macclenny reached major flood stage and peaked at 19.71 ft on Aug. 7th. 9.67 inches of rainfall was measured by a CoCoRaHS observer at Glen St. Mary 4.4 SW during Debby.

Keystone Heights Airport AWOS measured gusts between 40-52 mph during Debby. 6.22 inches of rainfall was measured by a COOP observer at 2.0 NE New River during Debby. The peak gust of 52 mph was measured at 3:35 am on 8/5 local time.

Multiple roads were inundated with floodwaters from Black Creek including Lazy Acres Rd and Scenic Dr. North Fork Black Creek near Middleburg rose to moderate flood stage and crested at 20.13 ft on Aug. 6th. South Fork Black Creek near Penney Farms rose to minor flood stage and crested at 15.54 ft on Aug. 6th. A large oak tree split at the trunk and fell across a lawn in Orange Park. There were two trees that fell and hit|homes and 15 residents reported storm damage to the county. 5.02 inches of rainfall was measured by a CoCoRaHS observer at Keystone Heights 10.0 NE during Debby.

Multiple downed trees and powerlines were reported blown down across the county. A tree snapped and fell on a car causing damage in Riverside. A large tree uprooted and fell on a house causing roof damage along Ribault Scenic Dr. Edgewood Ave was closed due to flooding. Wind gusts between 40-62 mph were observed during Debby. 6.29 inches of rainfall was measured by a CoCoRaHS observer at Jacksonville 11.3 WNW during Debby.

SR-26 was closed at the Gilchrist and Alachua County line due to flooding. SR-47 from NE CR-340 to SE CR-232 was closed in Gilchrist County due to downed trees, powerlines, and flooding. Peak wind gust of 42 mph was measured by 0651W 4.7 W Newberry  WEATHERSTEM) on 8/5 at 5 am local time. 10.32 inches of rainfall was measured by a|CoCoRaHS observer at 5 W Newberry during Debby.

Tropical cyclone wind gusts impacted the county on 8/5. Wind gusts between 40-54 mph were observed during Debby. At 5:58 pm on 8/4, the mesonet at Marineland measured a wind gust of 54 mph. At 6:20 am on 8/5, the station measured 41 mph wind gusts. Flagler county EMA reported a few trees were downed in Palm Coast and Bunnell.

The county experienced gusts of tropical storm force and flooding rainfall with 11.63 inches of rainfallmeasured by a CoCoRaHS observer at White Springs 0.3 NW during Debby. Wind gusts between 41-44 mph were observed during Debby. At 6:20 am local time on 8/5, a mesonet station 3 miles SSE of Jasper measured wind gusts of 44 mph. At 6:30 am, a mesonet station 6 miles NE of Suwannee Springs measured a wind gust of 41 mph.
AWOS station KOCF Ocala Airport gusted to 41 mph during Debby on 8/5 at 1:14 am local time. A CoCoRaHS observer measured 9.37 inches of rainfall at Micanopy 3.6 SSW during Debby.

Nassau County Emergency Management reported that Stokes Road bridge was closed due to being inundated by river flooding on the Georgia side of the St. Marys River. St. Marys river also flooded the Scott���s Landing boat ramp and nearby sheds at St. Marys river campground. The St. Marys River near Macclenny reached major flood stage and peaked at 19.71 ft on Aug. 7th. The St. Marys River at Traders Hill reached|major flood stage and peaked at 16.17 ft on Aug. 10th. Zidell Road in Callahan was closed due to deep floodwaters making it impassable. A car was also stranded in the floodwaters. CR-119 and CR-121 were reported flooded but passable. 9.27 inches of rainfall were reported in Hilliard, FL during Debby. The AWOS station KFHB Fernandina Beach gusted to 46 mph.

Widespread downed trees and powerlines were reported across the county. A tree fell on a home and caused unknown damage. A road was reported to be washed out. 4.56 inches of rainfall was measured by a CoCoRaHS observer in Hollister during Debby. The AWOS site at Palatka Airport (K28J) measured a peak wind gust of 47 mph on 8/5 at 12:35 PM.

Wind gusts between 50-58 mph were observed during Debby and 7.28 inches of rainfall was measured by a CoCoRaHS observer at Sawgrass 0.0 E during Debby. On 8/4 at 9:10 pm local time, the mesonet station in downtown St. Augustine measured a wind gust of 44 mph in an outer rainband.

Suwannee was the most heavily impacted county in the NWS Jacksonville area as the eyewall of Debby crossed over the county through the day on 8/5. Widespread flash flooding occurred with water inundation into structures and swift water rescue deployments. Most of the City of Live Oak was flooded and the southern end of the county was inaccessible for some time after the storm. Most businesses in the city of|Live Oak were flooded and a major county road was completely washed out near the Community of Wellborn. U.S. Highway 90 was closed for about 36 hours. The Miami-Dade Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) Team was deployed to the southern end of the county with the initial push south and a large Incident Management Team (IMT) effort was set up in Live Oak. Extensive tree and structure damage was observed county-wide. Major main stem river flooding was occurring on both the Suwannee and Santa Fe Rivers. On 8/5 at 3:40 am local time, a wind gust of 40 mph was measured in Dowling Park and at 4:40 am the gusts were 41 mph. By 5:10 am, the gusts strengthened to 48 mph then 49 mph at 6 am. At 6:15 am on 8/5, the Suwannee Airport AWOS gust to 46 mph and at 6:20 am the mesonet in Dowling Park measured a gust of 53 mph. On 8/5 at 12:20 PM, a peak wind gust of 65 mph was observed at FAWN Suwannee Advent Christian Village WeatherSTEM site.

Most of the county's impacts included wind damage and flooding. On 8/5, State Warning Point relayed that the City of Lake Butler reported an ongoing raw sewage release of approximately 3,000-4,000 gallons from the wastewater treatment plant due to a lightning strike on the generator. No storm drains or waterways were impacted. SW CR-231A in Lake Butler was closed due to large fallen trees along the road. 7.22 inches of rainfall was measured by a COOP observer at 3.6 NW Lake Butler during Debby. The EM reported that the WeatherStem station at the county courthouse in Lake Butler measured 9.99 inches of storm total rainfall and had a peak wind gust of 45 mph during Debby. On 8/4 at 7:40 PM, one of Debby���s rainbands produced a severe tornadic thunderstorm. The tornado was rated an EF1 and touched down about a quarter of a mile south of State Road 238 and about a quarter mile east of Southwest County Road 241 and moved northwest towards Southwest 85th Path. The tornado produced EF1 tornado damage at 7:40 PM as it touched down south of State Road 238 by snapping the tree trunk of a large hardwood tree. The tornado proceeded northwest to homes along Southwest 85th Path, overturning a travel trailer, knocking down a wooden fence, and uprooting another hardwood tree. The tornado's last impact was tearing off the roof of a shed along Southwest 85th Path before it lifted. The tornado was on the ground for about 1 minute and was on the ground a distance of just under a quarter of a mile. The tornado had a maximum width of about 20 yards and had maximum winds up to about 93 mph.

Appling County Emergency Management reported at least 6 dirt roads washed out by floodwaters, including Jim Sellers Road at the intersection of U.S. Highway 341, Zoar Road, and Hill Top Road. Over 130 road closures or roads inundated by floodwaters were reported throughout the county. A storm total rainfall of 14.7 inches was measured at the City of Baxley Water Treatment Plant as of 4 PM on August 6th. A large|earthen dam broke near Piney Bluff Road and drained an estimated millions of gallons of water leveling small trees and grass in a nearby field, almost inundating a nearby mobile home, flooding US HWY 1 with about 2.5 to 3 feet deep of floodwater, and then washed out Hill Top Road sweeping culverts into the woods. A property along Oak View Drive experienced 4-5 feet of flood water inundation from the dam break. This caused water inundation into a shed, damage to power tools, a golf cart and lawnmower. A large Oak tree fell across Hershel Tillman Road making it impassable.  On 8/6 at 1:35 am local time, the EM reported that US 1 North between Kate Mann Road and East River Road was closed due to water over the road.

Multiple road closures were reported due to flooded roads. Multiple locations along County Road 170 near Axson, GA were washed out and collapsed. Deep flood water along Lige Road and Wood Duck Rd made them impassable. W Albany Ave in Pearson, GA also suffered extensive flooding with floodwaters approaching business doors. 5.54 inches of rainfall was measured by a CoCoRaHS observer at Pearson 3.5 NE during Debby.
Alma, Bacon County Airport (KAMG) measured a peak wind gust of 40 mph on 8/6 at 12:42 AM.

Widespread road closures and washed out dirt roads occurred due to flooding rainfall. Dryden St, Fort Mudge Rd, Eastwood Rd, and Thrift Rd were washed out and scoured by floodwaters. A van was stranded in flood water along Post Rd. A few small trees fell across Wyatt Rd. 7.69 inches of rainfall was measured by a CoCoRaHS observer at Nahunta 6 S during Debby.
Multiple dirt roads were washed out across Camden county. A large tree uprooted at Sanctuary Golf Club. 8.8 inches of rainfall was measured by a CoCoRaHS observer at Kingsland 1.2 WSW during Debby.

Nassau County Emergency Management reported that Stokes Road was closed due to being inundated by river flooding on the Georgia side of the St. Marys River. An uprooted tree fell on a home in Clinch county. Downed trees and powerlines were reported. 5.74 inches of rainfall was measured by a HADS site at Fargo during Debby.

Multiple dirt roads were reported to be flooded including Club Road. 4.93 inches of rainfall was measured by a CoCoRaHS observer at Douglas 2.5 WSW during Debby. Wind gusts between 42-52 mph were observed during Debby.

The College Park neighborhood in Brunswick was one of the most flooded areas in the city. Water entered homes. Several trees fell and damaged homes in Brunswick with some homes having roof damage due to metal roofing material being peeled off. One outbuilding was destroyed due to a large tree that fell on it. 5.8 inches of rainfall was measured by an AWOS site at Brunswick Golden Isles Airport (KBQK) during Debby.|Wind gusts ranged between 44-57 mph. On 8/4 at 5:57 pm, a mesonet site on Jekyll Island measured a wind gust of 48 mph in an outer rainband. At 10:15 pm, at ASOS at the St. Simons Island Airport measured a wind gust of 44 mph.

Flash flooding occurred county wide with the most washed out roadways being dirt roads. Two swift water rescues were required, the first an individual whose car was swept off an asphalt county road and the second was a woman who drove around barriers into a flooded dirt road. One of these rescues was along Towns Bluff Road on Tuesday morning, 8/6. One structure flooded in the City of Hazlehurst in a known flooding trouble area. School was closed for several days until sanitation facilities and dirt roads were brought back online. 4.54 inches of rainfall was measured by an AWOS  site at Hazlehurst Airport (KAZE) during Debby. AWOS station Hazlehurst Airport (KAZE) also gusted to 41 mph.

Trees and powerlines were blown down.

At 6:05 am, major flooding along Deep Creek was occurring near Hastings with around 5.5 ft MHHW reported. This site reaches major flood stage at 4.2 ft MHHW. Widespread flooding rainfall combined with storm surge was caused widespread flooding across the area, including within the city limits of Hastings. At 6:07 am, major flooding was impacting communities near Haw Creek where widespread flooding rainfall was attempting to drain in the St. Johns river basin, but the river was surging limiting drainage. Several homes were surrounded by flood water and some homes had flood water damage.

Widespread flooding rainfall combined with rising storm surge which disabled drainage in and near the City of St. Augustine caused flash flooding. At 5:15 am, the EM reported flooding across the city roads. At 5:19 am, Anastasia Island was flooded on the north side across Highway A1A including in the Davis Shores area.
At 10:30 am, law enforcement had to close State Road 20 in Palatka due to flooding. This is a major artery through the city.

Widespread flash flooding due to rainfall of 5-8 inches in the morning caused roads, agricultural fields and some structure flooding from Hastings to Flagler estates. At 10:30 am, EM shared a picture of flood water across Alvin Street in Hastings. At the same time, a vide of flood waters from Moccasin Creek Lane was shared from near Elkton by the media. This flooding rainfall was from the approach of Milton south of the area and a local nor'easter.

The highest wind gusts in Alachua county were 49 mph in Gainesville, and 47 mph at the University of Florida main campus. The 49 mph was measured at 1:53 am on 10/10 by the KGNV Gainesville Regional Airport ASOS. Widespread 2-3 inches were reported across the county. Two public shelters opened ahead of Milton and both reached capacity, prompting a third shelter opening.
The highest wind gust in Bradford county was 40 mph at the Keystone Heights airport.

Clay county received about 2-3 inches of rain across the county, with the highest storm total northeast of Keystone Heights at 3.76 inches. There were reports of surge flooding from the St. Johns river resulting in road closures near the intersection of Plainfield Avenue and Lakefield Lane in the Orange Park area and Williams Park Road near the boat ramp adjacent to the St. Johns River south of Green Cove Springs. On Oct. 10th at 6:24 PM EDT, the St. Johns River at Buckman Bridge river gauge reached major river flood stage and measured a peak height of 3.01 FT MHHW. There were also reports of trees and powerlines down.

In a rainband ahead of Hurricane Helene, a weak tornado formed|near Broxton, GA along George Deen Rd and HWY 268. A video of the|tornado was posted on social media. Minor structural damage to |homes and several trees down were reported in this area. Around 2:30 pm, the tornado was sighted on the ground near Highway 268 East. It damaged shingles and shifted a doublewide trailer off of its foundation at 2507 and 2807 Highway 268 East. Multiple trees were blown down with confirmed damage as 1668, 1700 and 1732 George Deen Road. Some trees fell on a home.

Between September 9-13th about 12 inches of rainfall fell across the Penial/Francis area (11.82 was measured at Moates Road on 9/13).  A location at 111 Penial Store Road experienced overflow from lakes in the area. This property was flooded given it's low elevation location downstream of the flooded lakes. Public works identified a crushed 36 culvert in the area of Penial Store Road and the Dinkla Road area. Water from the local lakes caused rainfall to back-up into Mud Lake and it could not drain. Impacts from this flooding event included: at Mud Lake Farm on NW corner of Mud Lake was impacted by water into the Barn/Garage (EM Verified); at 134 Karen Court flood water was in the backyard from Mud Lake and against the home (EM/Red Cross verified); a home at 111 Peniel Store Rd had possible water intrusion and the kitchen roof collapsed (unconfirmed damages, owner not present nor responsive to EM or Red Cross); a home at 116 Green Rd had minor water intrusion into the basement and water came through the floor and walls underground (EM Verified); and a garage had water into it at 263 Davis Lake Rd (EM picture confirmation). All other information and complaints have been for water near homes, next to homes, in yards, or over roads.

Several days of training, heavy rainfall caused areal flooding in the Palatka city limits. By 9/15, flood water was over the road along Alabama Avenue. A home near the intersection of Highlawn Ave and 3rd Avenue experienced flood water impacts related to a blocked culvert not draining water. This home was located in a low-lying area per county Public Works.

At 2 am on 9/27, the EM reported multiple county wide calls of citizens trapped in homes. Highest gust recorded in the county was 53 mph from the NNW at about 1:50 am on the 27th, via Atkinson County EMA Weatherstem site. A manufactured home was completely destroyed in Willacoochee along US 82 near Sutton St and Paulk Ave. A large tree fell on a house destroying the roof in Kirkland. The roof was lifted completely off the Atkinson Court house and shingles were peeled off on the surrounding buildings.  A warehouse suffered extensive damage in Pearson. The Georgia Farm Bureau reported numerous flattened or damaged chicken houses in Atkinson county.

The Alma GA ASOS owned and maintained by the NWS JAX office reported a sustained 56 mph with a gust near 100 mph from the SSE at 3:30am. There was significant damage to a couple of roofs and the building facade along 12th St in Alma, GA. A large tree fell and destroyed a trailer in Alma.  ||On 9/27 at 2:08 am, the ASOS station at the Bacon County Airport in Alma measured a gust of 86 mph. At 2:49 am, the ASOS measured a wind gust of 91 mph which was the highest thus far on record at that location.  At 3:03 am, the sensor measured a gust of 100 mph from the SSE, the all-time record wind gust of this location. A nearby UGA Weatherstem site also measured a max gust of 88mph from the SSE at about 2:45am.

The entirety of the county was out of power on the morning of the 27th after the storm. Numerous trees and power lines down throughout the county with many road closures. Notable max gusts via Weatherstem sites:  51mph from the S at about 2:15 am (Nahunta), 58 mph from the SSE at about 2:20am (Waynesville). The same Waynesville site also reported sustained tropical storm force winds of 45 mph out of the SSE at 2:40 am.

Widespread trees and power lines down in the county, with some road closures. Multiple large trees and tree limbs fell on homes causing roof damage in Saint Marys. Schools remain closed as of Monday the 30th. Notable max wind gusts via Weatherstem sites: 45mph from the SE at 1:30am (Woodbine), and 53 mph from the S at about 3:19 am (Cumberland Island).
Widespread trees and power lines down in the county, with some road closures. Notable max wind gusts via Weatherstem sites: 45mph from the SE at 1:30am (Woodbine).

About 30% of homes were still without power in the county as of Monday the 30th, and cell service was ���nearly non-existent in many areas���. Schools remain closed as of the 30th. A number of trees and power lines down throughout the county, including many transformers blown a large tree wrapped in power lines across the road near Martin St. A Weatherstem site in the NW Okefenokee Swamp measured a gust to 64 mph out of the SSE at about 2:10am.

About 30% of homes were still without power in the County as of Monday the 30th, and cell service was ���nearly non-existent in many areas���. Schools remain closed as of the 30th. A number of trees and power lines down throughout the county, including many transformers blown a large tree wrapped in power lines across the road near Martin St.

Widespread downed trees and power lines were reported across the county. Many cars and houses were damaged or destroyed by falling trees, especially in Homerville along E Dame Ave, and US 441. Over 400 power poles were broken. The community opened four Good Samaritan shelters. A Weatherstem site in Homerville measured a max wind gust of 63 mph from the SSW at about 2:45 am on the 27th. 100% of the county was without power following the storm. One person was killed, and another person was injured due to trees falling onto mobile homes.

At 2:30 am on 9/27, a mesonet site 2 miles SSW of Baxley measured a gust of 68 mph from the SE.  At 3:38 am, a mesonet station 2 miles SSW of Baxley measured a wind gust of 73 mph from the S. Widespread power outages, numerous trees down, powerlines down, and minor damage to homes were reported. Some large trees fell on homes causing roof damage. A metal roof was completely blown off a building in Baxley. Appling county emergency management implemented a curfew beginning September 30th to support public safety efforts for the widespread power outage, disruptions to cellular service and damaged traffic signals. The Georgia Farm Bureau reported numerous flattened or damaged chicken houses in Appling county.

Widespread downed trees and power lines were reported across the county, especially along GA HWY 32. Many roads were blocked due to downed trees and powerlines across the county. There were numerous reports of structural damage and fallen trees on residences destroying roofs and causing some entrapments. Schools to be closed through at least October 4th. There was one fatality due to a tree falling directly on a mobile home and killing one person inside. ||On 9/26 around 2:33 pm, the EM reported and a video confirmed a Tornado about 1 mile NNE of Broxton on the ground near Highway 268. Minor structure damage occurred including shingles blown off and a double-wide trailer was shifted off of its foundation at 2507 and 2807 Highway 268E. Multiple trees were blown down with confirmed damage at 1668, 1700 and 1732 George Deen Road. Some trees fell and destroyed a carport and caused some damage to the home.  ||At 1 am on 9/27, the public reported several trees were blown down in a yard in Pridgen. At 2 am on 9/27, the EM reported the roof was blown off of a shelter in Nicholls. Injuries were unknown at the time of the report. In Douglas, there was extensive roof damage with metal roofs blown off of manufactured homes, shopping centers, businesses, and the City of Douglas fire station.  Widespread uprooted and snapped trees fell on homes and manufactured homes in the Douglas area, especially along Walker St, Gaskin Ave, and Golf Club Rd. This resulted in widespread significant roof damage with numerous homes��� roofs and walls collapsing from the fallen trees. High winds also caused the total destruction of multiple mobile homes. A school along GA-158 in Douglas suffered a collapse of their concrete-block hallway structure, a significant portion of the roof was blown off and debris scattered across the grounds, and part of the concrete walls were destroyed.  Windows were blown out and carports collapsed in Douglas. In Nicholls, a cell phone tower was knocked down and destroyed along Sessoms Rd. The Georgia Department of Agriculture (GDA) reported that 100 poultry farms in Coffee County were affected by the storm with numerous reports of flattened or damaged chicken houses. ||A Weatherstem site east of Douglas reported a sustained wind of 46 mph with a gust to 92 mph from the SE at about 2:15 am.

A Weatherstem site in Lake Park measured a wind gust of 90 mph out of the SE at about 1:00 am Friday the 27th. A shelter in place was issued by the county on Thursday Afternoon (26th) ahead of the storm. Approximately 1000 power poles were broken in the county, almost twice of what occurred during Hurricane Idalia in 2023. Widespread trees and powerlines were down throughout the county: described as ���unprecedented historic damage��� by EMA. Many roads were blocked by trees and powerlines and many roofs were damaged by both high winds and fallen trees, especially along HWY 129.

Widespread trees and power lines were blown down across the county. Multiple uprooted trees caused damage to power lines, cars and homes. Over 36000 without power as of early Friday morning (27th). A couple of gas station canopies either collapsed or were knocked over in Brunswick. |On 9/26 at 11:15 am, a mesonet site on Jekyll Island measured a wind gust of 44 mph. On 9/27 at 12:22 am, a mesonet station on Jekyll Island measured a wind gust of 69  mph. At 1:52 am, the site measured a wind gust of 78 mph from the SE. At 2:15 am, the ASOS KSSI on St. Simons at the McKinnon Airport measured a wind gust of 68 mph from the SE.

Widespread trees and power lines were blown down across the county. Multiple uprooted trees caused damage to power lines, cars and homes. A church spire topple to the ground along US 341 and Depratter Ln in Sterling, GA. Over 36000 without power as of early Friday morning (27th).

Widespread trees and powerlines were down throughout the county, many across roads and homes causing entrapments. At 2:15 am on 9/27, the EM reported a fatality in a mobile home. A follow-up media report indicated that there was a male and female killed in a mobile home along Highway 19 at Adams Cemetery Road when the trailer was lifted off of its foundation and thrown into a nearby field. A tree fell on a mobile home along Bell Telephone Road and killed one person inside per a media report. Another person was reported missing. About 85% of county residents were without power. Many businesses in Hazelhurst suffered roof and awning damage. A large tree fell on a home along US 221 causing the roof to collapse. The Georgia Farm Bureau reported numerous flattened or damaged chicken houses in Jeff Davis county.

A Blackshear firefighter was killed in the line of duty when a tree fell onto his truck when he was responding to calls during the night of the hurricane in Blackshear, GA. Widespread trees and powerlines down, restoration of power is slow due to damage and extent. A shelter was opened after the storm to provide a safe place for people to stay, and a Red Cross shelter was opened to hand out supplies. The Georgia Department of Agriculture reported that a table egg producer in Pierce County had 17 houses down.

At 1:50 am on 9/27, a mesonet station at the Wayne County High School about 2 miles NW of Jesup measured a 66 mph wind gust from the SE.  At 3:20 am, a mesonet station about 1 mile NNE of Jesup along US Highway 341 at State Road 38 measured a gust of 64 mph from the SE. Widespread trees and powerlines down across the county, with wind damage to homes like shutters, shingles, and trees fallen on homes. A significant portion of the metal roofing of a local school peeled off. The county experienced 100% power outage and some households didn���t have power for 14 days.

At 2:04 am on 9/27, the RAWS station OKEG1 in Waycross measured a wind gust of 71 mph from the SE. Reports of widespread power outages, no running water, powerlines down, trees down, and damage to mobile homes.  Ware County opened two shelters in Waycross before the storm. In Waycross, widespread uprooted and snapped trees fell on roads, cars, and houses, especially along Seminole Trail, St. Marys Dr, Cherokee Dr, and Satilla Blvd. This resulted in multiple houses having their roofs destroyed.

At 2:04 am on 9/27, the RAWS station OKEG1 in Waycross measured a wind gust of 71 mph from the SE. Reports of widespread power outages, no running water, powerlines down, trees down, and damage to mobile homes.

A male drowned in a rip current on Sunday, 10/12 at Mickler's Landing.

Local broadcast media reported that St Johns County Fire Rescue pulled a woman from out of the ocean near the Ponte Vedra Inn and |            Club. The woman was taken to the hospital in |            critical condition.
Minor street flooding was observed in the |            Southhampton neighborhood on Alamo and Bee |            Streets during high tide.

At 8:40 AM EDT, an NWS employee reported that there was extensive flooding on Philips Highway and Bowden Road. At 10:40 am, broadcast media shared that flood water inundated a home in Englewood and went up to the person's ankles. Widespread street flooding with numerous cars reported as submerged and stranded along roads or ditches. A swift water rescue was conducted to rescue a person stuck in their flooded car with floodwater up to their steering wheel. Multiple roads were closed due to flooding including Sabena Road and Bowden Rd at Richard St and Cagle Rd. Floodwaters went over car wheels or halfway up cars wheel base along Richard St, Bowden Rd, Barnes Rd, Kegler Dr, Revelstroke Dr, Philips Hwy, Reba Ave, Parental Home Rd, Spring Park Rd, Dean Rd, Belfort Rd, Putnam Ave, Vancouver Dr and portions of University Blvd.

Flagler County had Hurricane force wind gusts mainly along the coast ranging from 45-92 mph which led to downed trees and powerlines as well as roof damage being reported across much of the county. It should be noted the 92 mph wind gust reported at a WeatherStem site at Marineland remains suspect. The combination of heavy rainfall and surge flooding led to extensive flooding across Flagler county. ||Widespread 5-9 inches of rain were reported, with the highest storm total measured at 9.36 inches in Bunnell at 1:10 am on 10/10. At 2:53 pm, Flagler EM reported flooding in the city on the west side of the bridge on West 100 by the railroad tracks. At 3:30 pm on 10/9, a CoCoRaHS observer about 5 miles NW of Palm Coast reported 2.54 inches of rainfall since 6 am with a flooded yard. On 10/10 at 2:16 am, a mesonet site 3 miles S of Palm Coast had measured 5.51 inches of rainfall. At 3:23 am, a mesonet site 4 miles SE of Andalusia measured 6.05 inches of storm total rainfall. ||On Oct. 10th at 5:15 PM, the Pellicer Creek near Espanola river gauge peaked in moderate flood stage and measured a height of 3.14 ft MHHW. The Flagler EM reported the salt water canals were 23 inches over the top in Palm Coast. Widespread street flooding, flooded docks, and road closures were reported across Palm Coast due to heavy rainfall and storm surge. Floodwaters inundated a home along Perthshire Ln in Palm Coast with floodwaters reaching up to a woman���s ankles. Floodwaters in the streets appeared to reach halfway up a car���s tire. According to the Flagler Sheriff, a swift water rescue of a family was conducted in Palm Coast when their truck became stranded in floodwaters. Street flooding from rainfall as well as overflow from creeks, canals, and lakes were present across the inland portions of the county. ||Haw Creek above Russell Landing near Crescent Lake reached major flooding on Oct. 10th at 2:30 AM and then reached record flooding at 9.23 ft on Oct. 12th at 12:15 PM. This record level broke the previous record of 8.7 ft set during Hurricane Irma. According to the Flagler Sheriff, a swift water rescue of a lady and her pets was conducted due to floodwaters from Haw Creek inundating her home along CR-305. The floodwaters surrounding the house went up to the knees of police officers. Waters from Bull Creek flooded the nearby Bull Creek Fish Campgrounds. Due to a large amount of accumulated water over the highway at the base of the overpass in Bunnell, FDOT closed the road between Woodland Street and Deen Road. Flooding was also reported in Bunnell on the west side of the bridge on West 100 by the railroad tracks. ||Numerous trees were reported down across roads and on power lines in Bunnell and Palm Coast. A snapped tree fell on a home along Lloyd Trail in Palm Coast and destroyed the roof. Another tree fell on a car in the W Section of Palm Coast and totaled the car. Fences were damaged either by strong wind gusts or fallen trees in Palm Coast. A screened enclosure was damaged by a fallen tree along Courtney Pl in Palm Coast. At 10:10 PM, 1334W 1.6 E Palm Coast WeatherSTEM station measured a wind gust of 50 mph with sustained wind of 40 mph. At 11:35 pm, the AWOS at the Bunnell Airport reported a gust of 51 mph. At 11:55 PM, AWOS station KFIN Flagler County in Bunnell reported a wind gust of 54 mph. On 10/10 at 12:55 am, the AWOS at the Bunnell airport measured a wind gust of 55 mph. At 1:25 am, a mesonet site about 3 miles ENE of Bunnell reported a sustained wind of 54 mph. ||NOTE: The Marineland mesonet site was on the higher end of observations, even higher than some gusts reported near the eyewall closer to Cape Canaveral. Flagler County Emergency Management reported that the county suffered an estimated $18.8 million in damages.

The St. Johns River tributary Deep Creek at Spuds, in southern St. Johns County, crested in major flood stage at 5.94 ft MHHW on October 10th at 2 PM EDT. This broke the prior record water level that was established during Hurricane Irma in September 2017. This record flood level was mostly due to rainfall runoff from the widespread 5-9 inches of rainfall that fell across southern St. Johns County combined with elevated tides. Water levels at this gauge near the town of Hastings were above what is considered major flooding from around sunset on Wednesday, October 9th through 12 PM on Saturday, October 12th. The Flagler Estates and Hastings communities were severely impacted with extensive flooding, which began on 10/9. At 9:55 am, county EM reported flooding along Alvin Road in Hastings. At 10:30 am, media reported flood water was across Moccasin Creek Lane near Elkton. The county EM reported at 7:32 pm that roads and fields from Hastings to Flagler Estates were covered in flood waters. The St Johns Sheriff Office reported numerous roads that were closed for multiple days and impassable due to flood waters in the vicinity of Hastings and Flagler Estates including East Deep Creek Blvd, Ashley St, Flagler Estates Blvd, East St. Johns Avenue, Catherine St, Dillon Ave, and Morrison Road. Many homes were surrounded by flood waters. ||Widespread power outages and trees down were reported down across the county, as well as significant damage to barns. At 12:09 am on 10/10, St. Johns County Fire Rescue reported flood water was flowing over the intersection of Flagler Estates Blvd and East Deep Creek Blvd. This flooding was due to a combination of Storm Surge into Deep Creek and flooding rainfall. At 11:45 pm, the Deep Creek gage at Spuds reported a water level of 4.87 ft MHHW datum. Major flooding for this location begins at 4.2 ft MHHW. At 10:10 AM on 10/10, the Emergency Management team reported that water was across County Road 13 near Six Mile Creek, which is a tributary of the St. Johns River. Mostly continuous rainfall led to widespread 5-9 inches of rainfall that fell for areas mainly along and south of St. Augustine and Elkton. Marion county received about 3-9 inches of rainfall from Milton across the county. The highest rainfall amounts were south of Ocala where a CoCoRAHs observer measured 9.42 inches of storm total rainfall. On 10/9 at 8:22 pm, the public measured 4.15 inches at Shady Airport in Ocala. Downed trees and powerlines were reported around the county, with the highest wind gusts ranging from 40-46 mph in Ocala, Lake George, and the Villages. The strongest gust of 46 mph was measured by a mesonet site 3 ESE of the Ocala Airport on 10/10 at 12:50 am. An uprooted tree destroyed a RV in the Wandering Oaks RV Park off of US-301 and FL-326 in Ocala.

Marion county received about 3-9 inches of rainfall from Milton across the county. Downed trees and powerlines were reported around the county, with the highest wind gusts ranging from 40-46 mph in Ocala, Lake George, and the Villages. A home near Rainbow River was destroyed due to a fallen tree and one person suffered non-life-threatening injuries. A downed tree east of Canton Farms fell across the roadway and blocked a lane on County Road 484. The entire city of Dunnellon lost power during Milton.

Major to minor damage was reported across the county, both from wind damage as well as river and rainfall flooding. Many homes had significant wind damage to roofs, fences, and carports. Extensive flooding of streets and homes occurred for areas along the St. Johns River and its tributaries including Dunns Creek due to the combination of rainfall runoff and elevated tides. The St. Johns River in Putnam county entered moderate flood stage on the evening of Oct. 9th evening and then major flood stage on Oct. 10th. On 10/10 at 10:30 PM, Dunns Creek near Satsuma crested in major flood at 3.32 feet MHHW and the St. Johns River at Buffalo Bluff also crested in major flood at 3.14 feet MHHW. The entire Sportsman Harbor neighborhood near Welaka was completely flooded with floodwaters from the St. Johns River inundating homes and trapping residents in their homes. County officials had to use boats and amphibious vehicles to deliver supplies and reach residents. Floodwaters appeared to reach up to people���s knees. Flooding continued through Oct. 13th. Floodwaters from the St. Johns River also inundated multiple homes along Beechers Point Dr near Welaka. Flooded and impassable streets due to the St. Johns River flooding were also reported in Federal Point including Commercial Ave. Major flooding along Dunns Creek in Satsuma flooded streets near the creek making them impassable including Marina Ln, Edgewater Rd, and Walt Ln. Floodwaters from Dunns Creek inundated homes along Paradise Cir and Magnolia Tr. Floodwaters along Paradise Cir went halfway up a woman���s calves. Clay county received about 2-3 inches of rain across the county, with the highest storm total northeast of Keystone Heights at 3.76 inches. On Oct. 10th at 4:30 PM EDT, the South Fork Black Creek near Penney Farms gauge reached 16.87 FT, just below moderate flood stage. Creek St and Black Creek Dr were underwater and docks along South Fork Black Creek were underwater and damaged. There were also reports of trees and powerlines down.

Duval county reported wind gusts of 40-64 mph, with the highest of 64 mph at Mayport Naval Station. The St. Johns River in downtown Jacksonville reached moderate flood stage, and near the Buckman Bridge reached moderate to major flood stage. Street flooding in Riverside, Southampton, and Pottsburg Creek were reported. events.cz_name: FERNANDINA BEACH TO ST AUGUSTINE FL OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: St. Johns County Emergency Management relayed a photo of a waterspout that approached the shore near Vilano Beach, FL. This waterspout was also reported by personnel at the Northeast Florida Regional Airport in St. Augustine, FL.
Mesonet station GW3621 BLACKSHEAR measured |            over 4.61 inches of rain in just over an |            hour.
Private weather station near Waycross |            measured 4.49 inches of rain in about an |            hour.

At 5:45 pm, the public shared a video shared via social media of minor flooding near Alice Street, including standing water and a vehicle partially submerged. Around the same time, the public shared images and video via social media of flooding in southeast Waycross, including parking lots with standing water and partially submerged vehicles.

Coastal flooding was reported along Glynn Ave at the intersection with F J Torras Causeway. Nearby tidal gauges measured peak tides of 2-2.7 ft MHHW. Fort Pulaski, GA - Station ID: 8670870 tidal gauge measured a peak tide of 2.74 ft MHHW at 6:30 AM on 11/14/24.
The public observed a funnel cloud near Grand Haven.

In Grand Haven in Palm Coast, a screen lanai |            was damaged from wind blown debris, with |            small twigs and branches down. Possible |            small gustnado ahead of line of showers and |            thunderstorms. Information was relayed |            through EMA. Time of event was estimated.  The cost of damage was unknown but it was estimated for inclusion in storm data.
The AWOS at Naval Station Mayport measured a wind gust of 59 mph.

At 1:30 am on 1/22, county emergency management reported a fire engine truck rolled over on County Road 108 near Hilliard due to icy roads. At 7:30 am, a Center Weather Service Unit employee reported tree limbs were broken and across vehicles in Hilliard due to heavy ice accumulations.

At 7:45 am on 1/22, Nassau County Emergency Management reported that the State Road 200 Bridge over the Intracoastal Waterway (Shave Bridge) was closed due to ice accumulation. Multiple accidents were reported across the county due to hazardous driving conditions. At 8:19 am, the public shared a photo via social media of sleet about 0.7 inches thick in Yulee. At 8:30 am, Nassau County Emergency Management and the Florida State Watch Office reported that Interstate 95 in the vicinity of State Road 200 was closed in both directions due to a vehicular accident with an injury. Semi-trucks also jackknifed and crashed on I-95 near the US-17 exit blocking the off ramp and part of the lanes. At 9 am, the public reported 0.3 inches of snow and ice accumulation in Fernandina Beach.

Tropical Storm Fay moved slowly north out of Caribbean Sea, then cut across south and central Florida into the Atlantic Ocean. Fay then slowly curved west and made landfall in the vicinity for Flagler Beach and Daytona Beach on Aug 21st. As the storm made landfall sustained winds along the coast were between 40 and 50 mph with gusts in the 60 to 65 mph range. Storm Surge ranged from 2 to 4 feet along the open coast and about 1 to 2 feet on the St Johns River.  Storm Surge Flooding occurred on the St Johns River on Thursday night August 21-22 in the Palatka area of Putnam County as northeasterly winds created a seiche effect driving river water southward.  On Friday morning August 22nd the winds became more southeasterly along the river and river water was driven north in the San Marco and Riverside areas of Downtown Jacksonville flooding roadways and some structures. River water depths of 4 to 6 inches flooded the Park Lane Condominium in Riverside. A Ford Bronco in the street outside of the condo floated in the river water a short distance into Memorial Park. Flash flooding occurred on McCoys Creek on Thursday night and Moncrief Creek on Friday. Both creeks are in Jacksonville, Duval County, Florida.  Several vehicles were stranded at Kings Road and McCoys Creek Blvd including one vehicle up to its roof. Areal flooding occurred over much of northeast Florida with roads and small creeks flooded. Minor flooding of structures occurred across the area. Numerous trees and power lines were downed with minor structural damage. High surf and beach erosion threatened five homes on the 3850 block of S Ponte Vedra Blvd in Vilano Beach, Florida. Several minor tornado touchdowns occurred in the area with no significant damage or injuries. Many north Florida creeks and Rivers experienced fresh water flooding with Black Creek, The St Marys River at McClenny, the St Johns River, south of Palatka, and the Sante Fe River experiencing the most significant flooding.

Georgia Forestry Commission responded to a wildfire caused by a downed powerline at approximately 3:00 p.m. this afternoon north of Folkston along Hwy 301. Upon arrival, the fire was estimated at 100 acres. The wildfire increased to an estimated 697 acres and stretched nearly 2 miles from U.S.-301 to County Road 252. Two homes received minor damage and eight minor structures were destroyed. Charlton County EMA reported evacuations due to the wildfire near Hwy 301 / Humphries Rd Area in Folkston. Roads under evacuation orders included Harold White Road, Humphries Road, Bill Knight Road, Willow Creek Road.

Powerline broke from non-thunderstorm winds near the 8000 block of Highway 301. Peak wind gusts during the day were around 45 mph. This led to the development of the wildfire that spread southeastward just north of Folkston.

At the beginning of February, Florida Forest Service reported a wildfire of about 318 acres near State Road 20 that then increased to 400 acres and persisted through February 24th. On February 4th and 6th, the Putnam County Sheriffs Office reported that a combination of thick smoke and fog (smog or superfog) resulted in the closure of State Road 20 in the vicinity of Keuka Road. This closure extended to County Road 315 South to Lake Galilee. Schools were also closed on February 4th and 6th due to school bus route cancellations. On February 10th, Putnam County SO advised that CR-20 A, locally Keuka Road, was closed at Strickland Rd due to heavy smoke from the Pace Ct wildfire.

Flagler County Emergency Management reported that a 170 acre wildfire in the vicinity of Korona along U.S. Highway 1 South forced the evacuations of 25 residences and 1 building on Wednesday evening. Evacuation orders in the area were lifted at midnight.

On February 7th, Marion County Fire Rescue reported a 1 acre wildfire near Ocklawaha which then quickly grew to 172 acres before being 100% contained on February 12th. An unknown number of residences were advised to evacuate due to the wildfire.

On March 23rd, Alachua County Sheriff's Office reported that a small brush fire that ignited near S County Road 325 near Cross Creek. This fire quickly grew in size to 134 acres by the end of the month thanks to very favorable fire weather conditions.
A wildfire near Cross Creek, FL of 134 acres remained ongoing during the month of April, increasing containment to approximately 75% by the end of the month.

The Sargent wildfire  developed in northwest Baker county, northern Osceola National Forest on April 2, 2026 around 350 PM EDT. The smoke plume extended northward affecting local roads near the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge and into Waycross, GA. On April 3rd, the Florida Forest Service reported the Sargent Fire quickly grew to about 4,000 acres moving into Columbia and Clinch counties. The highway between Fargo, GA and John Bethea State Forest in Florida was closed (Highway 2 in Florida and Highway 94 in Georgia). The majority of the fire was burning in Florida but it had crossed into southern Georgia. On the evening of April 3rd, the fire was now estimated at 2,720 acres and 50% contained following improved mapping. On April 5th, Florida Highway 2 and Georgia Highway 94 were now only closed at night due to potential low visibility from fog and smoke. Light rain on April 5th and 6th was not enough to help put out the fire. On April 11th, the fire was 81% contained at 2,489 acres. On April 15th, reburn in the swamp occurred due to hot and dry weather. On April 20th, the acreage increased to 2,523 acres due to spotfires which are caused by flying sparks or embers carried by the wind from an existing fire and ignite a new fire. No structures were threatened. Breezy winds, extreme to exceptional drought conditions, lack of beneficial rain, and remaining heavy fuels continued elevated fire activity through the month of April.

Bradford County Fire responded to a wildfire in Booker on the 21st of April, which grew to 205 acres during the next several days thereafter. The fire continued to burn through the end of the month, reaching maximum containment of about 60%.

A wildfire near Sanderson quickly grew to 500-600 acres during the 12th of April, also prompting 4 evacuations near Doyle Williams Road. These evacuations were then lifted on the 13th of April. There are little details known beyond this date, however it is likely the wildfire continued to burn through the end of April.

The Pace CT wildfire continued through the month of March at 318 acres with 75% containment.

Per Florida Forest Service, a wildfire that was burning during the end of March continued into early April near Taylor. The wildfire was at 366 acres with 90% containment on the 1st of April. Details are limited thereafter, but was likely contained by the end of the month.

The Pace CT wildfire continued through most of April at 318 acres with 75% containment. On April 21, the fire grew to 343.35 acres with 85% containment. The fire continued to burn through the end of the month.

A wildfire ignited near Conner-Nelson Rd in Hilliard on the 14th of April, resulting in the evacuation of one residence and a closure of County Road 115 nearby as a result of poor visibility from smoke. The fire grew to 500 acres shortly thereafter. By the evening of the 22nd of April, the fire was almost fully contained and all road closures had been lifted.

On April 19, 2026 around 530 PM EDT, Clay County EM reported a 100 acre wildfire in Green Cove Springs with 0% containment. Evacuations occurred at Varney Rd and Woodward Rd due to the wildfires located along Crews Rd in Clay County and north of Bostwick in Putnam County. The wildfires were 1700 acres combined between the two counties. On April 20 at 6 PM EDT,  Florida Highway Patrol reported a Road Closure of US-17 and Varney Rd due to the ongoing Wildfire in Green Cove Springs. US-17 reopened later that evening. On April 21st, the Florida Forest Service decided to combine the Crews Rd Fire in southeast Clay County and the Railroad Fire in northeast Putnam County into the Railroad Complex Fire. The combined new total acreage was 4112 with a 50% containment. On April 28, the fire was at 4,796 acres with 80% containment. Breezy winds, extreme drought conditions, lack of beneficial rain, and dry fuels continued elevated fire activity through the month of April. The cause of the fires were believed to be from humans.

On the 18th of April, the Pineland Road fire ignited over southern Clinch County, rapidly growing to 2500 acres by the 19th of April due to favorable conditions. The area of Fargo Highway to Tiger Lake Road was urged to prepare to evacuate as a result. Evacuations expanded to the Colon area on the 21st of April, as the fire reached approximately 16500 acres in size. By the 22nd of April, the fire reached about 32183 acres in size, and at least 5 roads in Clinch County were closed. Impacts from smoke reached areas such as Homerville and Fargo by the 27th of April due to a change in wind direction, as the fire continued to burn at approximately 32540 acres in size. By the 29th of April, Clinch County Emergency Management released a 3 level map featuring evacuation zones due to the fire, with a large area of thousands of acres under a mandatory evacuation. The fire reached 40% containment by the evening of April 30th. The estimated cost of the wildfire was around $14-15 million.

By the 20th of April, the Pineland Road fire wildfire that ignited over southern Clinch County crossed into Echols County, with several roads north of route 94E told to prepare to evacuate.  The fire grew to 16500 acres by the 21st of April, with a mandatory evacuation issued for Will Rewis Rd and Chauncey Rd. By the 22nd of April, the fire reached about 29600 acres in size, and the Fruitland area was added to the mandatory evacuation. By the 26th, the fire had grown to 32000 acres and 14 roads were closed in Echols County as a result. A report from the Georgia Forestry Commission on the 28th of April stated that 187 residences and 123 other minor structures remained threatened as the fire remained around 32000 acres in size. The fire reached 40% containment by the evening of April 30th. The estimated cost of the wildfire was around $14-15 million.

On April 20, 2026 at 4 PM EDT, the Georgia Forestry Commission reported a wildfire developed along Highway 82 near Atkinson, GA. The Highway 82 fire was caused by a Mylar balloon coming into contact with a power line, creating an electrical arc that ignited the surrounding vegetation. This wildfire resulted in the worst home loss from a single fire in Georgia history, with 110 homes destroyed and 27 homes damaged. At 7 PM EDT, a voluntary evacuation was requested for those North of Hwy 82 to the East and West of Hwy 110 and was then extended northward up GA-110. On April 21st at 5 AM, the fire was 700 acres and 75% contained per the GFC. Portions of Highway 82 were closed due to heavy smoke from the active flames. Winds shifted from southerly to easterly through the day causing the fire to go from spreading north to then spreading westward. At 1 PM, a Mandatory Evacuation for Browntown Rd, Hawks Landing Neighborhood, Warners Landing, Oaks Woodlands, Atkinson Road, Godberry Lane, Brushing Creek, Fort Mcintosh to Highway 520 on both sides of the road was issued by Brantley County Emergency Management Agency. Brantley County Sheriff���s Office and Glynn County Sheriff���s Office also closed the road at Hwy 82 from Nahunta to Post Road, GA-110 at Highway 32 down to the Camden County line, Hwy 259 from Highway 82 to the Camden County line, and Hwy 32 from Highway 110 to Post Road. Mandatory evacuations continued into the evening and were issued for Happy Hollow, Drury Ln, Drury Ct, Coffee County Club Rd and From Thrower Rd to Mossy Oak as the fire grew quickly to 5,000 acres. The County Manager for Brantley County reported that at least 42 structures were burned due to the Highway 82 Wildfire. On April 22nd, mandatory evacuations continued for Browntown Road from Greenleaf Rd to Hwy 32. On April 23rd, Brantley County Sheriff's Office stated that the wildfire was estimated to be roughly 5,000 acres with 15% containment. The combination of heavy smoke and dust significantly reduced visibility for first responders, creating an extremely dangerous situation for both the public and emergency personnel. Mandatory Evacuations were then issued for the area of Hwy 110 from Hwy 32 to Lane Cemetery Rd to include from Lisa Ln to the Satilla River. On April 24th, the fire was 7,566 acres per the National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC). At 1PM, Georgia DOT closed SR 32 from Hortense to SR 99 due to fire and heavy smoke in Brantley County. On April 25th, the fire grew to 9,578 acres per overnight infrared flight mapping. The winds shifted to southwesterly pushing smoke from Brantley County to Glynn County, with heavy smoke around Post Road and Highway 32. Evacuation areas were expanded to the Brantley���Wayne County line due to the fire movement to the north and northeast, while evacuations and road closures on the southern portion of the fire have been lifted. Wayne County issued Mandatory Evacuations for the area from the Brantley County Line at Wire Rd to Post Rd, to Ten Mile Rd and all areas in between. The fire was 13,745 acres and 7% contained. The fire produced 150-foot flame lengths during a significant run toward Browntown Road. The blaze was a plume-dominated wildfire, a rare occurrence that happened on multiple days during the fire. On April 26th, a Mandatory Evacuation was issued for the entire community of Manningtown, off of Browntown Road by Wayne County Emergency Management. Glynn County EM also issued Mandatory Evacuations for Old Post Road to Highway 32, Highway 32 to Thalman Park Lane, Thalman Park Lane to Bladen Road and Bladen Road to Old Post Road. Infrared mapping showed the fire had doubled within 24 hours at approximately 20,933 acres with 7% containment. Without precipitation, the fire was very active again with wind driven movement to the northeast and east until the wind shifted in the afternoon with the sea breeze. At 5 PM, Wayne County EM announced the fire had crossed into Wayne county. At 8 PM, an isolated thunderstorm moved over the fire bringing rain amounts of 0.4 to 0.8 inches. This amount of rain did not extinguish the fire, but briefly decreased the extreme fire behavior. On April 27th, winds shifted to north-northeasterly which led to Glynn county downgrading evacuations and re-opening previously closed roads. On April 28th, the fire was 22,600 acres and 32% contained. On April 30th, roads from Browntown south of Murphy Road and HWY 32 were opened. The fire was 22,532 acres and 37% contained. More smoke occurred on April 30th in bay vegetation due to hot and dry conditions, extended long-term drought and lack of rain. A new fire started north of the Hwy 82 Fire in Wayne County that was approximately 40 acres.

The fire produced 150-foot flame lengths during a significant run toward Browntown Road. The blaze was a plume-dominated wildfire, a rare occurrence that happened on multiple days during the fire. On April 26th, a Mandatory Evacuation was issued for the entire community of Manningtown, off of Browntown Road by Wayne County Emergency Management. Infrared mapping showed the fire at approximately 20,933 acres with 7% containment. Without precipitation, the fire was very active again with wind driven movement to the northeast and east until the wind shifted in the afternoon with the sea breeze. At 5 PM, Wayne County EM announced the fire had crossed into Wayne county. At 8 PM, an isolated thunderstorm moved over the fire bringing rain amounts of 0.4 to 0.8 inches. This amount of rain did not extinguish the fire, but briefly decreased the extreme fire behavior. On April 28th, the fire was 22,600 acres and 32% contained. On April 30th, roads from Browntown south of Murphy Road and HWY 32 were opened. The fire was 22,532 acres and 37% contained. More smoke occurred on April 30th in bay vegetation due to hot and dry conditions, extended long-term drought and lack of rain. A new fire started north of the Hwy 82 Fire in Wayne County that was approximately 40 acres.

On April 20, 2026 at 4 PM EDT, the Georgia Forestry Commission reported a wildfire developed along Highway 82 near Atkinson, GA. The Highway 82 fire was caused by a Mylar balloon coming into contact with a power line, creating an electrical arc that ignited the surrounding vegetation. This wildfire resulted in the worst home loss from a single fire in Georgia history, with 110 homes destroyed and 27 homes damaged. On April 25th, the fire grew to 9,578 acres per overnight infrared flight mapping. The winds shifted to southwesterly pushing smoke from Brantley County to Glynn County, with heavy smoke around Post Road and Highway 32. The fire was 13,745 acres and 7% contained. The fire produced 150-foot flame lengths during a significant run toward Browntown Road. The blaze was a plume-dominated wildfire, a rare occurrence that happened on multiple days during the fire. On April 26th, Glynn County EM issued Mandatory Evacuations for Old Post Road to Highway 32, Highway 32 to Thalman Park Lane, Thalman Park Lane to Bladen Road and Bladen Road to Old Post Road. Infrared mapping showed the fire at approximately 20,933 acres with 7% containment. Without precipitation, the fire was very active again with wind driven movement to the northeast and east until the wind shifted in the afternoon with the sea breeze. At 8 PM, an isolated thunderstorm moved over the fire bringing rain amounts of 0.4 to 0.8 inches. This amount of rain did not extinguish the fire, but briefly decreased the extreme fire behavior. On April 27th, winds shifted to north-northeasterly which led to Glynn county downgrading evacuations and re-opening previously closed roads. On April 28th, the fire was 22,600 acres and 32% contained. On April 30th, roads from Browntown south of Murphy Road and HWY 32 were opened. The fire was 22,532 acres and 37% contained. More smoke occurred on April 30th in bay vegetation due to hot and dry conditions, extended long-term drought and lack of rain.

Numerous power lines were blown down across Eastern Duval county.

Winds estimated at 55 to 60 mph were rocking a spotters car at 1100 11th Street SW in Live Oak.
A tree fell on a pool house near the Clinch County Airport.
Multiple trees were blown down on power lines from Fargo to 4 miles north of Fargo along Highway 441. The time of damage was based on radar.
A retired NWS employee reported a billboard was destroyed near Mariners Village about 6 miles east of Interstate 95 near Highway 40. The time of damage was based on radar.
An oak tree was blown down at the Harbor Pines Apartments on Harbor Pines Drive.
Numerous trees were blown down on Highway 40, about 2 miles east of Folkston.
A retired NWS employee reported numerous trees down and estimated winds of 60 mph in Bristol Hammock Plantation.
The EMA reported 22 large trees were blown down throughout the county. The downed trees landed on four homes, two businesses and four trailer homes. The event lasted about 12 minutes.
Winds were estimated at 60 mph. The winds destroyed a pump house which supplied water for the main house.
A tree fell on a trailer home and injured two residents inside. The victims were taken to the local hospital. The extent of their injuries was unknown.
A retired NWS employee reported a large oak tree and power lines were blown down off of Osborne Road. The time of the event was based on radar.
A weeping willow tree was uprooted at 10 Aviation Lane at the FAA Control Center in Hilliard.

Lightning struck a transformer at the corner of Atlantic and Monument Roads. The power lines caught fire and feel onto a car stopped at the traffic light. Two men rescued the driver of the car that was burning. A local gas station had to shut down their pumps due to the lightning fire. The victim did not suffer critical injuries.

A spotter reported widespread wind damage across Sugarmill Plantation including downed trees and limbs, fence damage and roof damage. He heard of a report of a roof blown off of a construction trailer at a local school.
Golf ball size hail was reported north of Fargo.
Penny size hail was reported in Argyle.

Penny size hail occurred in Uptonville. A power line was also blown down along Dixie Union Highway through Uptonville.
Penny and dime size hail was reported at 405 West 11th Street.
Golf ball to penny size hail was reported in Alma.
Penny to dime size hail was reported at the corner of Dixon Street and West 12th Street. The time of the reported was approximated.
The U.S. Highway 1 Convenience Store said a customer along Hatch Parkway North reported penny size hail. The time of the report was based on radar.
Penny to dime size hail was reported in Colesburg. The time was based on radar.
A spotter reported a tornado north of Fargo. The circulation tracked east and snapped tree tops.
The Echols County Emergency Management received several reports of trees blown down. Most of the damage was in the western part of the county.
A large tree was blown down in Tarboro and power was out in the local community. Trees were also blown down in Dover Bluff.
A funnel cloud was reported near Peanut Mills along SW Railroad Avenue.
A Kangaroo Express employee was traveling east of Newberry and experienced hail penny to pea size along County Road 235. The time of the event was based on radar.
Quarter size hail was observed at the intersection of State Road 26 and State Road 21.
Penny size hail was reported near Florahome.
The Emergency Manager reported that 4 to 5 inches of rain had fallen with many streets flooded.
A spotter measured 4.57 inches of rainfall from 1347 local time to 1520 local time.
Trees were blown down near White Springs. The time of the event was based on radar.
Widespread tree damage occurred in Gainesville. One tree was blown down at the intersection of a subdivision at 5113 NW 33rd Street which blocked access to the neighborhood.
A tree was blown down on a car at 3630 NW 71st Street just NW of Gainesville.
Trees were blown down across the road in the 6800 and 8300 blocks of NW 39th Street.
Two large outbuildings were destroyed by a downburst wind near County Road 302 just west of County Road 305. Debris struck a vehicle.

events.event_narrative: Lake Hampton Road was closed to flood water steadily leaving the lake. Most of the water that was leaving the lake was flowing under Lake Hampton Road  through culverts as the lake eventually drained into the St. Marys River. Several trees had been washed into the drainage basin area between the levee and culverts and the debris was being monitored to ensure that it did not clog the culverts.
The Flagler Beach Fire Department reported 6 to 8 foot surf at Flagler Beach.
A spotter saw a tornado while driving near New Post Road and Highway 252. The debris from the vortex damaged his windshield and damage trees in the area.
A spotter near Fargo reported several trees were blown down at his residence when the storm passed.
A spotter measured just under 8 inches of rainfall in 24 hours.

Tropical Storm Fay moved slowly north out of Caribbean Sea, then cut across south and central Florida into the Atlantic Ocean. Fay then slowly curved west and made landfall in the vicinity for Flagler Beach and Daytona Beach on Aug 21st. As the storm made landfall sustained winds along the coast were between 40 and 50 mph with gusts in the 60 to 65 mph range. Storm Surge ranged from 2 to 4 feet along the open coast and about 1 to 2 feet on the St Johns River.  Storm Surge Flooding occurred on the St Johns River on Thursday night August 21-22 in the Palatka area of Putnam County as northeasterly winds created a seiche effect driving river water southward.  On Friday morning August 22nd the winds became more southeasterly along the river and river water was driven north in the San Marco and Riverside areas of Downtown Jacksonville flooding roadways and some structures. River water depths of 4 to 6 inches flooded the Park Lane Condominium in Riverside. A Ford Bronco in the street outside of the condo floated in the river water a short distance into Memorial Park. Flash flooding occurred on McCoys Creek on Thursday night and Moncrief Creek on Friday. Both creeks are in Jacksonville, Duval County, Florida.  Several vehicles were stranded at Kings Road and McCoys Creek Blvd including one vehicle up to its roof. Areal flooding occurred over much of northeast Florida with roads and small creeks flooded. Minor flooding of structures occurred across the area. Numerous trees and power lines were downed with minor structural damage. High surf and beach erosion threatened five homes on the 3850 block of S Ponte Vedra Blvd in Vilano Beach, Florida. Several minor tornado touchdowns occurred in the area with no significant damage or injuries. Many north Florida creeks and Rivers experienced fresh water flooding with Black Creek, The St Marys River at McClenny, the St Johns River, south of Palatka, and the Sante Fe River experiencing the most significant flooding.

As the storm made landfall sustained winds along the coast were between 40 and 50 mph with gusts in the 60 to 65 mph range. Storm Surge ranged from 2 to 4 feet along the open coast and about 1 to 2 feet on the St Johns River.  Storm Surge Flooding occurred on the St Johns River on Thursday night August 21-22 in the Palatka area of Putnam County as northeasterly winds created a seiche effect driving river water southward.  On Friday morning August 22nd the winds became more southeasterly along the river and river water was driven north in the San Marco and Riverside areas of Downtown Jacksonville flooding roadways and some structures. River water depths of 4 to 6 inches flooded the Park Lane Condominium in Riverside. A Ford Bronco in the street outside of the condo floated in the river water a short distance into Memorial Park. Flash flooding occurred on McCoys Creek on Thursday night and Moncrief Creek on Friday. Both creeks are in Jacksonville, Duval County, Florida.  Several vehicles were stranded at Kings Road and McCoys Creek Blvd including one vehicle up to its roof. Areal flooding occurred over much of northeast Florida with roads and small creeks flooded. Minor flooding of structures occurred across the area. Numerous trees and power lines were downed with minor structural damage. High surf and beach erosion threatened five homes on the 3850 block of S Ponte Vedra Blvd in Vilano Beach, Florida. Several minor tornado touchdowns occurred in the area with no significant damage or injuries. Many north Florida creeks and Rivers experienced fresh water flooding with Black Creek, The St Marys River at McClenny, the St Johns River, south of Palatka, and the Sante Fe River experiencing the most significant flooding.

Tropical Storm Fay made landfall well south of the Georgia coast with strong winds, high tides, high surf and heavy rainfall impacting Glynn and Camden Counties. Heavy rainfall spread inland as Fay moved west causing some flooding across portions of interior southeast Georgia.

events.event_narrative: A mariner reported quarter size hail and estimated wind gusts to near 40 knots when he was about 35 nm northeast of Marineland. His vessel suffered hail damage.

A squall line moved across north Florida and into the Magaretta area. As the system moved into the area of Mack Ruise Road and Ruise Lane a microburst impacted the area with an estimated 60 to 75 mph sustained winds. One mobile home had a hole punched through its roof. A second structure, built largely of particle board with no reinforcing bracing, was unroofed with portions of the roof thrown approximately 100 yards to the north. The damage made this structure uninhabitable and it was the most severely impacted structure. A third structure had its sheet metal roof removed from the southern portion of the structure and thrown to the north. Two trees were snapped at the base and laid flat to the north. A witness described seeing a vortex and a second witness described being lifted off the ground by that vortex. These reports are consistent with a possible gustnado and it is believed that this is what contacted the most severely affected structure.
Several trees were blown down along path of storm. Vinyl fencing blown down with some shingles ripped off a roof. Two trampolines were  blown a considerable distance.

The tornado touched down near 1421 College Avenue destroying a vinyl storage shed. A more substantial wood shed next to it was undamaged and no significant damage to vegetation was observed in this vicinity.  In this area the event was a low level EF-0 event with winds estimated near 65 mph. The system next moved over Burney Branch Lake which allowed the circulation to intensify with winds now closer to an upper end EF-0 and estimated to be near 85 mph.  The tornado made landfall near 1101 Lakeview Drive where several trees were snapped. The funnel moved over several lakeside homes and their backyards in this area. A vinyl fence was blown down and a wooden child���s backyard play set was uprooted and overturned. At the northeastern edge of the lake the most substantial damage occurred when the roof of a dock was ripped off and blown onto the roof of a home at 919 Edgewood Circle.  The home���s roof was destroyed opening the contents to the weather.

Some of the debris landed in the front yard splicing an electric line in 2 places, the weight from the debris caused an electric pole to lean to the left. A second portion of the carport roof landed about 90 yards past the house in the tree line. The Suwannee County Emergency Management Agency determined the event to be due to Straight Line Wind and not a tornado. There were no other signs of visible damage to the residence or property.

The tornado touched down as an EF-0 in an open field just east of the Suwannee River and south of the Progress Energy power plant. It increased to intensity becoming a low end EF-1 tornado several hundred feet down track where it impacted several farm buildings and mobile homes. Several small farm structures were destroyed and winds here we estimated to be between 86 and 90 mph. The tornado continued moving northeastward as an EF-0 snapping trees along its path near the entrance to the Suwannee River State Park and along Stagecoach Road. It then went through a wooded area emerging along West Tower Road where it began the occlusion process. The rear flank downdraft heavily damaged two chicken houses with a loss of about a quarter million dollars. At this point the tornado took a northward turn toward the Jenkins Farm house destroying a large work shed with heavy machinery and damaging the home. The tornado was rated as an EF-1 here with winds of 95 to 100 mph. Debris from the shed was strewn across the field north of the Jenkins Farm house to Stagecoach Road.
