At 8:54 pm on the 27th, the Kings Bay Naval Base reported at wind gust to 58 mph in a rain band. At 10:35 pm, the emergency manager reported that Kings Bay had a gust to 65 mph on a waterfront facility before the wind sensor stopped working. There were also reports of several trees blown down in the area. At 11 pm, the emergency manager reported a vehicle accident due to a tree down in the road at Harriets Bluff Road and Paulk Place. At 12:20 am, the emergency manager reported a tree was blown down on a home on Gary Place in Kingsland. There were no injuries. At 12:30 am, the emergency manager estimated winds near 65 mph in Harrietts Bluff. Pine trees and large branches were blown down int he area. At 2:50 am, the public reported trees and power lines were blown down in Harrietts Bluff. At 7:20 am, a retired NWS Employee reported several large, healthy oak trees were blown down in the Bristol Hammock neighborhood. At 9:04 am, a NWS employee reported numerous large oak tree limbs about 2 to 2.5 inches in diameter were broken off near Borrell Blvd and Riverview Drive. At 12:06 pm on the 28th, the emergency manager reported that the city dock and boat ramp about 5 miles WSW of Dugeness were closed in downtown St. Marys due to significant damage.||The Kings Bay Naval Base lost a $2 million dollar dock. A total of $2.3M in damage from T.S. Beryl was estimated by the base.
The St. Simons island ASOS measured a wind gust to 43 mph.

events.cz_name: FERNANDINA BEACH TO ST AUGUSTINE FL 20 TO 60NM
events.event_narrative: The St. Augustine Buoy 41012 about 43 NM east of St. Augustine Florida first measured tropical storm force wind gusts at 11:16 am on the 27th with a gust of 52 mph. At  1:08 pm, the buoy measured wind gusts of 56 mph with sustained speeds of 37 mph. At 3:41 pm, the buoy measured at gust of 59 mph. Maximum sustained winds were 45 mph. At 4:54 pm, the peak gust at the buoy was 67 mph and maximum sustained winds were 51 mph. At 10 pm that evening, the buoy measured at gust to 60 mph on the back side of TS Beryl.

events.cz_name: FERNANDINA BEACH TO ST AUGUSTINE FL OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: At 6:30 pm, a mesonet site at Huguenot Park measured a gust to 54 mph with sustained speeds of 43 mph. At 9:21 pm, the buoy 6 miles east of Fernandina Beach recorded seas of 15 feet.

At 10:43 am, flooding was reported at 1596 Lancaster Terrace at the Broadview Towers Condos. The river rose similar to levels observed during TS Fay in 2008. A below ground parking lot was completely flooded with three cars floating. The river was breaking over the sea wall. Peak flooding at this location occurred between 4 to 5 am. At the same time, flooding was also reported at the corner of Copland St and Riverside Ave. Parts of the sea wall were removed and moved about 8 to 12 feet. A dock was destroyed and debris was dispersed throughout the area. The peak flooding at this location was between 5 and 6 pm.  The cost of damage was estimated.
At 4:40 pm, wind damage occurred to a shed and water pump northeast of Live Oak. At 5:10 pm at residence was damaged at 22207 41st Drive in Branford.
Nickel size hail was reported in Graham and the Spring Hill Branch Community.
Golf ball size hail was observed in Mershon.
Numerous trees were blown down. The time of damage was based on radar.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down in Mershon.
Trees were blown down along Old Waynesville Road.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down in the Bristol area.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down in Patterson.
Trees were blown down along Tupelo Circle near Highway 17.
A tree was blown down on Village Drive.
Trees were blown down at Peachtree Street and Beach Drive.
Quarter to nickel size hail was reported in Baxley.
Quarter size hail was reported along M & M Estates Road in Screven. The time of the event was based on radar.
Quarter size hail was reported on Parkwood Drive in Brunswick.
Nickel size hail was reported on Velie St and on Wilson Road.
Power lines were blown down on Cook St in Baxley.

Widespread flooding occurred across east Jacksonville. At 5:27 pm, local broacast media reported Central Parkway on the Southside was under several feet of water. At 6:01 pm, a NWS employee reported Debutante Road was flooded by 1.5 ft of water. Several cars were stranded in the flood waters. A spotter on Debutante Road measured 14 inches of rainfall within 24 hrs at 6:01 pm that evening. At 6:26 pm, the public reported 1 to 2 feet of standing water on Indies Drive. At 7:42 pm that evening, the broadcast media reported 9.5 inches of rainfall that day near Kernan Blvd and Beach Blvd.  The cost of property damage was estimated for inclusion of the event in Storm Data.
An observer reported 7.5 inches of rainfall on Fleming Island since 12:30 pm that afternoon.
An employee measured 7.31 inches of rainfall within 24 hours. Ditches were near bank-full and there was minor street flooding in the area.

A spotter reported moderate street flooding near the Veterans Administration Hospital in the Lake City. Storm drains were overflowing. Widespread 5 to 6 inches of rain fell throughout Suwannee and central portions of Columbia counties.
Rainfall accumulations were estimated around 3 to 3.25 inches in eastern Duval County. Ponding of water was observed on Atlantic Blvd. near the intersection with Girvin Road.
Portions of University Blvd were closed near the intersection of Philips Highway due to significant flooding.
Portions of San Marco Blvd in downtown Jacksonville were inundated by more than a foot of standing water.

Between 3:17 pm and 4 pm local time, significant flooding was reported in the Mandarin area and near Fruit Cove. At 3:17pm, minor street flooding was reported along Scott Mill Road between Indian Hill Drive and Bridalwood Lane. At 4 pm, flooding was reported over several roads which were nearly impassable near Julington Creek Road. Water was over yards but not into homes yet. Another spotter reported flooding in Fruit Cove, with numerous yards flooded but no homes. The cost of damage was estimated.
Dime to nickel size hail was reported along with minor local street flooding.
Nickel size hail occurred in northwest Palm Coast.
Quarter size hail was observed in northern Palm Coast.
Lightning struck a home and caused a fire. The extent of damage was unknown and the cost of damage was estimated.
Trees were blown down on State Road 13 North.
Penny size hail was reported south of Bostwick along U.S. 17.
A tree was blown down and blocking State Road 11 south of Bunnell. The time of event was based on radar.
Trees were blown down in power lines in East Bunnell. The time of damage was based on radar.
Several trees were blown down in Palatka.
Several trees were blown down in Crescent City.
Florida Power and Light Utility Company reported several trees down.
Quarter size hail was observed.
Trees and power lines were blown down near 6281 Old Dixie Drive in St. Augustine.
Several eight to ten foot trees were blown down.
A spotter reported that Florida Park Drive is flooded due to overflowing swales in north Palm Coast.
Quarter to dime size hail was observed.
Quarter size hail was reported at J. Turner Blvd. and Southside Blvd.
A strong microburst wind gust of 68 mph was recorded at the Naval Air Station Jacksonville ASOS.
Trees were blown down in a neighborhood which knocked out power. Some trees landed on homes.
Numerous trees were blown down near Baymeadows, Belfort Road and Philips Highway.
Power lines were blown down onto a home due to trees being blown down on the power lines.
Numerous trees were blown down in Southern Glynn County on Meyers Still Road.
Trees were blown down on power lines. This resulted in a fire on Mckinnon Road in White Oak.
Trees were blown down on the Laurel Island Links Golf Course. The time of damage was based on radar.

events.cz_name: FERNANDINA BEACH TO ST AUGUSTINE FL OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: A Weatherflow Station at the Jacksonville Beach Pier measured a wind gust from the south of 42 mph.
Reba Street was flooded near Philips Highway and the street was closed. Water was waist deep and property was flooded. The time of the causative event was based on radar.
Several trees were damaged in a strong storm. The cost of damage was estimated.

A tire store, made of a steel building, had its roof blown off due to a down burst wind entering the structure through 3 of its open bay doors. All debris was outspread in a uniform direction. A plant nursery across the street had uniform damage as well. The cost of damage was estimated.
Nickel size hail was reported on State Road 21 northeast of Hawthorne.
A tree fell down after being struck by lightning in Bulow. The coat of damage was estimated.
Trees were blown down along Highway 20 at Gordon Chapel Road.
The general public measured 2.49 inches of rain in 45 minutes near Fort White.
A spotter measured 2.4 inches of rain in one hour.
Trees and power lines were blown down. One tree landed on a mobile home. No injuries were reported.

A trained spotter at 2:30 am reported Anvers Road, amongst many across the Jacksonville Westside were flooded and impassable. At 3 am, an emergency manager reported of Suwannee county reported widespread roads across Live Oak as well as other more rural areas had severe flooding. Northern portions of Live Oak were evacuated due to flood waters. At 5 am, an NWS Storm Survey report observed severe flash flooding in White Springs of Hamilton county. Roads were washed out to a depth of 8 to 12 feet. The first road washed out was 1st Street in White Springs which was completely severed. The water then flowed along a stream bed to Jewett Street which was also completely severed to a depth of 12 feet. One culvert pipe was completely washed away and was not recovered. Kendrick Street was then flooded and approximately 20 feet of road bed was washed away or undermined. The cost of damage was estimated.
A couple of homes were under water about 12 miles south of the Suwannee River. The cost of damaged was estimated and is likely underestimated.

Around 6:30 pm, reports of widespread flooding across the Jacksonville Westside and portions of northern Clay county poured into the NWS office. At 6:30 pm, the public reported a part of a yard under water and water rising quickly due to a clogged drain about 5 miles WSW of downtown Jacksonville on the Westside. At 6:50 pm, flood waters entered a home on 105th Street between Blanding Blvd and Jammes Road on the Westside. At 7 pm, the public reported water in a home on West 22nd Street. At 7:10 pm, the public reported 1-2 feet of standing water at the intersection of Port Street and Melba Street. Also at 7:10 pm, the public reported flood waters in 2 homes on Antoinette Lane on the Jacksonville Westside. At 7:20 pm, the public reported a car was stranded due to flooding on Rensselaer Road. At 7:30 pm, the public reported standing water about 1 to 2 feet deep over Betsy Drive. At 7:35 pm, the public reported 2-3 feet of standing water over Columbus Ave. The water was overflowing into yards. At 9:02 pm, the public reported water was over the road on the 3600 block of Post Street and was lapping at the doors of homes. The cost of damage was estimated, and is likely under-estimated.

At 6:45 pm, an NWS employee reported 1 foot of standing water over the I-295 and Blanding Blvd exit in Orange Park. At 6:46 pm, the public reported street flooding near Whitey's Fish Camp, about 2 feet deep. At 7:08 pm, the public reported around 1 foot of standing water near Blanding Blvd and Tanglewood in the Lakeside area. At 7:15 pm, the public reported over a foot of standing water at Timbermill Lane and Timberlake Drive. Water was over-flowing out of the storm drain. At 8:20 pm, the public reported flood water coming up to home porches near Bradford and Old Kings Road on the Jacksonville Southside. At 8:30 pm, the public reported a retention pond overflowed and water was almost inside a home. At 9:26 pm, the public reported major flooding at an apartment complex near San Jose and Hartley Road with water about 4 to 5 inches deep inside the apartments. The resident had to be rescued. At 9:45 pm, the public reported knee to waist deep water on the 3100 block of Stonebriar Ridge Road in Oakleaf Plantation. The cost of damage was estimated, and it is likely an under-estimate.

At 10 pm, the public reported flooding on Sawpit Road on Black Hammock Island. At 1010  pm, the public reported flooding into a home on Rose Street, about 5 miles south of the Jacksonville International Airport. At 10:42 pm, the public reported flooding over Catoma Street in Orange Park. Water was over the street and up to doors of houses. Residents evacuated. The cost of damage was estimated, and it is likely an under-estimate.

On the 24th, the forestry service in Trenton measured 3.25 inches of rainfall since midnight that morning. On the 25th, at 8:47 am, a cooperative observer measured 6.10 in 24 hours about 4 miles NW of Bell.

At 8:50 am on the 24th, a spotter reported flooded streets in Belleview. At 9 am, a spotter measured 4.5 inches of rainfall in Fairfield since midnight that morning. At 12:06 am on the 25th, a spotter measured 7.92 inches of rainfall on June 24th (a 24 hours total) about 6 miles south of the Ocala Airport. On the 25th at 10:21 am, a newspaper in Marion county reported State Road 40 in Ocala was closed due to high water. At 1:20 pm, the pubilc reported 10.25 inches near the Fellowship area in NW Marion county during the past 24 hours. At 5:15 pm that afternoon, a CoCoRaHS observer about 3 miles SSW of Micanopy reported 1.10 inches of rainfall in 30 minutes. Marion county had extensive problems with sinkholes, with an estimated 52 due to heavy rainfall from TS Debby. The cost of damage was estimated, and is likely a large under-estimate.
Large tree branches were blown down over Southeast Robinson Road near Lake Lillian. The time of the event was based on radar imagery.
Six to seven structures including barns with some roofs blown off, were damaged. The damage began on Highway 326 and NW 80th Avenue and tracked north for 1.5 miles. The cost of damage was estimated.
Trees were blown down in Yulee and other parts of the county's east side. The time of damage was based on radar.

Part of a sheet metal roof was torn off at a hanger at Jacksonville International Aiport hangar at 14600 Younge Drive. Minor damage to an airplane and hangar door occurred. Also, a parking lot booth was blown over.

Widespread flooding occurred across Jacksonville. On 6/25 at 3:17 am, an NWS employee reported minor street flooding along Shindler Drive between 103rd Street and Collins Road in Jacksonville. At 7:11 am, the public reported 8 inches of water in a home at 6314 105th Street in the Normandy area of Jacksonville. At 8:04 am, an NWS employee reported 7.4 inches of rainfall in Arlington, about 6 miles west of Jacksonville Beach. At 10 am, Duval county emergency management reported flooding at a home in the Boone Park area of Riverside. There were about 40 road closures at the time across Duval county due to flooding. At 9:09 pm, a spotter reported flooding in the Country Roads Mobile Home Park about 4 miles NW of Orange Park. On 6/26 at 8:11 am, a spotter reported 4.25 inches of rainfall in the past 12 hours. There was about 9 inches of storm total rainfall with minor street flooding. At 3:53 pm, a NWS employee reported the intersection of 103rd Street and Shindler Drive was closed due to high flood water. At 5:45 pm, the public reported a creek was overflowing into home on Old Plank Road. The water depth was about 18 inches. At 6 pm, the public reported road and yard flooding along Blackthorn Road. At 7:02 pm, 12 to 18 inches of water was over the road about 3 mile WSW of Ortega due to a nearby creek out of its banks. At 8:30 pm on the 26th, a retention pond overflowed and water was approaching a home on Collins Ridge Blvd. On 9/27 at 6:34 am, Duval County Emergency Management reported the intersection of Garden Street and Imeson Road was flooded with at least one foot of standing water.  The cost of damage was estimated, and it is likely greatly under-estimated.

Widespread flooding occurred across Starke. At 7 am on 6/25, emergency management reported several roads under water in the city including Bessent Road near Valley Road, Colley Road near the Hospital, NE 14th Ave, NE 17th Ave, SR 230 and at SR 16 and Old Lawtey Road. At 7:38 am, Alligator Creek over flowed with several homes threatened by flood waters. U.S. Highway 301 was closed from State Road 16 to Market Road due to flooding. Additional flooding concerns included North Water Street, East Mimosa Drive and Branford Drive in Starked. Flood control gates on Lake Sampson were opened due to high lake levels. There were 7 inches of rainfall during the past 24 hours across the county. At 8:47 am, a co-operative observer in Starked measured 6.5 inches of rainfall in the past 24 hours. The cost of damage was estimated, and it is likely greatly under-estimated.
Flooding reports were reported along State Road 100 near Palatka. Some trees were also blown down due to saturated grounds. The cost of damage was estimated.

Tropical Storm force wind gusts started to impact Duval county on 6/24 at 3:33 pm in tropical squalls. At 3:33 pm, a mesonet site at Jacksonville Beach measured a wind gust to 46 mph from the south with a sustained speed of 30 mph. At 3:41 pm, the Naval Station Mayport measured a gust to 44 mph. At 2:09 am on 6/25, the Mayport Naval Station ASOS measured a gust to 44 mph. At 2:36 am, that same station measured a gust to 45 mph. At 6:57 am, the ASOS at Naval Air Station Jacksonville measured a wind gust to 51 mph.

At 9:15 pm on 6/24, strong wind gusts blew down trees and power lines in Flagler Beach. Emergency Management reported a power line blown down on South Central Avenue in Flagler Beach. At 9:32 pm, emergency management reported a tree down on power lines on Ramblewood Drive in Palm Coast. On 6/27 at 12:09 am, a spotter in west Palm Coast reported 7.20 inches of rainfall from 8 am to midnight.

Flooding impacted much of Suwannee County. On 6/25 at 7:30 pm, law enforcement reported flooding at U.S. Highway 90 at County Road 137 in Wellborn. The intersection was closed due to deep water. At 7:30 pm, the public reported 8.5 inches of water accumulation in Live Oak. At the same time, a trained spotter reported reported streets were beginning to flood due to ditches over-flowing toward the roadway in Live Oak. At 8:02 pm, law enforcement reported a tree was blown down in the right lane of Interstate 10 near mile marker 292 due to saturated grounds and gusty winds. On 6/28 at 10:23 am, an NWS Storm  Survey reported a sinkhole 1 block from the Intersection of Highway 90 and State Road 129. A few structures were in danger of being engulfed into the expanding sinkhole.  The cost of damage was estimated and is likely grossly under-estimated.
At 11:48 pm on 6/24, the St. Augustine Airport AWOS measured a wind gust to 42 mph. At 12:50 am on 6/25, the same station measured a gust to 46 mph.

At 7:26 am the park service reported a 24-hour rainfall total of 4.1 inches about 2 miles east of Lake City. At 9 am on 6/25, law enforcement reported eastbound Interstate 10 at mile marker 301 was closed due to high flood waters. At 9:15 am that morning, law enforcement reported U.S. Highway 41 southbound was closed near Interstate 10 due to flood waters. At 9 pm, law enforcement reported Interstate 10 eastbound at mile marker 301 was closed due to standing flood waters. At 8:16 am on 6/26, a co-operative observer reported a 24 hour rainfall total of 8.77 inches in Lake City. On 6/28 at 3:57 pm, the public reported a monthly rainfall total of 27.55 inches with 19.99 inches between the 23rd-26th about 5 miles northeast of Ichetucknee Springs.  The cost of damage was estimated, and is likely greatly under estimated.

Record flooding occurred in Baker county with a historic crest on the St. Marys River due to persistent heavy rainfall over NE Florida and SE Georgia in the river's upstream charge basin. Radar estimated that 15 to 25 inches fell in the charge basin over several days. On 6/25 at 9:32 pm, a spotter reported 3.46 inches of rainfall in the past 5 hours at a location 3 miles ESE of Sanderson. Ditches were at capacity in the area at the time of the report. At 10:25 pm that evening, the media reported 4.08 inches of rainfall since 5 pm that afternoon in Glen St. Mary. Water was crossing roads west of Glen St. Mary. At 10:30 pm, the media reported Interstate 10 eastbound at mile marker 317 near Sanderson was closed due to flooding. At 10:44 pm, Interstate 10 westbound at mile marker 324 near Glen St. Mary was closed due to flooding per a media report. Flooding continued through the end of the month. On 6/28 significant river flooding ensured on the St. Marys with numerous mobile homes flooded and a total loss. Other homes were also flooded. At 10:50 am, baker county emergency management reported a bridge floating down the St. Marys River.  At 1:06 pm, the State Road 121 bridge was flooded by the St. Marys River and was closed. The County Road 127 bridge over Cedar Creek collapsed. The cost of property loss was estimated and is likely greatly under-estimated.
A trained spotter about 5.5 miles west of Gainesville Regional Airport reported 6.55 inches of rainfall since 8 pm Sunday evening.
A co-operative observer measured 6.58 inches of rainfall in 24 hours.

Widespread flooding occurred across Hamilton county. At 9 pm on 6/25, law enforcement reported flooding at U.S. Highway 129 at County Road 150 in Jasper. At 6:43 am on 6/26, a CoCoRaHS observer about 5 miles WSW of Jennings reported 11 inches of rainfall. NW 13th Drive was flooded. At 8:16 am on 6/26 a co-operative observer reported a 24 hour rainfall total of 10.57 inches in Jasper. At 11:58 am that morning, another co-operative observer reported 13 inches of rainfall in about 12 hours about 7 miles north of White Springs. The cost of damage was estimated and is likely grossly under-estimated.
Tree tops were snapped at 4410 Tarragon Avenue in Middleburg. The cost of debris removal was estimated.
Old Jennings Road was flooded with water moving over yards. The cost of road damage was estimated.

The public reported U.S. Highway 90 was flooded and closed in downtown Live Oak. Several vehicles were stranded in flood waters in the downtown area. The cost of damage was estimated and is likely underestimated.

Widespread interstate flooding occurred along Interstate 10 in Baker County. The interstate was closed near mile marker 317 near Sanderson due to flooding. The cost of damage was estimated and is likely underestimated.

Significant flash flooding occurred in downtown Jacksonville. At 6 pm, the public reported yards and roads were flooded along Blackthorn Road. At 6:20 pm, emergency management reported several water rescues ongoing at the time. The cost of damage was estimated.
An observer measured 4.10 inches of rainfall in 1.5 hours.
An observer measured 4.92 inches of rain within 24 hours at Steven Foster State Park.
An observer measured 3.51 inches of rainfall in 24 hours.
A former NWS employee measured 6 inches of rainfall since 6 am on Sunday.
A former NWS employee measured 5.70 inches of rainfall within 24 hours. The 48 rainfall total at his location thus far was 11.70 inches.
The rainfall total since midnight was 3.59 inches. An additional 4.88 inches was measured on Monday June 25th.
Trees were blown down on a car. Two power lines were also blown down. The time of damage was based on radar.
A thunderstorm wind gust to 61 mph was measured.
Homes on Thrift Road were surrounded by approaching flood waters. The cost of damage was estimated.

Widespread river flooding continued in southern Camden county due to historic flooding on the St. Marys River from heavy rainfall courtesy of Tropical Storm Debby. State Road 40 was closed between Kingsland and Folkston due to flooding. Numerous residences in Flea Hill were flooded and evacuated. About 37 homes in the Flea Hill area were flooded with river waters. The total cost of damage is still unknown, and for this recorded was estimated.
A citizen was struck by lightning and taken to the hospital.
Numerous trees were blown down in Hazelhurst. The time of damage was based on radar imagery.
Power lines were blown down near the county farm plant outside of Baxley. The time of damage was based on radar.
Trees were blown down near Martin Luther King Drive in Baxley. The time of damage was based on radar.
Trees were blown down from thunderstorm winds. The time of the event was based on radar.
Trees and power lines were blown down. The time of damage was based on radar imagery.
Trees and power lines were blown down across the county. The time of damage was based on radar imagery of the outflow gust front.
Eight to ten trees were blown down across the county along with 4-5 transformer blown down. The power was out in St. Marys. The time of wind damage was based on radar imagery.
Power lines were damaged along Fire Line Drive from thunderstorm winds. The time of event damage was based on radar.
Trees and power lines were blown down on the west side of Waycross. The time of damage was based on radar imagery.
Quarter size hail was reported.
Quarter size hail and gusty winds were reported at a restaurant in Georgetown. The time of hail was based on radar imagery.
Quarter size hail was reported on the Live Oak Golf Course.
Quarter size hail was reported on the Live Oak Golf Course.
Trees were blown down in Anthony. Small hail was also observed.
Trees were blown down at 259 Chesser Road.
Winds of 60 mph were estimated in Keystone Heights.

Nickel size hail and tree debris was observed.

Penny size hail was reported at 122 Behm Circle.
Power lines were blown down along Pine Avenue between Hibernia and Water Oak Lane.
Two funnel clouds were sighted near Highway 326 and Interstate 75.
Trees were blown down and blocking State Road 100 in Andalusia.

A lightning strike caused damage at a business at NW 13th St in Gainesville. The time of the fire was based on radar and lightning data. The cost of damage was unknown and estimated for inclusion in Storm Data.
Dime size hail was reported at NW 16th Ave in Gainesville.
Power lines were blown down in Keystone Heights.
Trees were blown down at the intersection of US Highway 90 and Cow Pen Road near Sanderson. The time of the event was based on radar.
Trees were blown down over Turner Cemetery Road near Sanderson. The time of damage was based on radar.
Trees were blown down on County Road 235. The time of damage was based on radar.
Nickel size hail was observed. The time of the event was based on radar.
Trees and power lines were blown down along Johnsons Lake Road near Rockingham. The time of the event was based on radar.
Quarter size hail was reported in Marion with wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph which caused tree debris.
Storm total rainfall within 2 hours was 2 inches.
A roof was blown off of an outbuilding and a trampoline was blown into the woods nearby. About 1/4 mile away from this structural damage, some trees were blown down. The cost of damage was estimated.
Trees were blown down near the town center of Ambrose.
Large trees were blown down on 2 homes on Birmingham Ave in Nicholls.
A large tree was blown down and blocked Old Graham Road. The time of the damage was based on radar.

Trees were blown down east of Dowling Park and Luraville which caused partial road blockage. The time of damage was based on radar data.
Trees and power lines were damage. A corn field was damaged due to a microburst. The event time was based on radar.

Trees and power lines were blown down along Harlow Road on the Westside of Jacksonville. The tree was about 12 inches in diamater. Power lines were also blown down along Tom Thumb Drive. The time of damage was based on radar, and the cost of damage was estimated.
Trees were blown down along Highway 1 in the Waycross city limits. The time of damage was based on radar data.
Power lines were blown down along Brunel Street in south Waycross.
Parkers Gas Station reported trees blown down along the Jesup Highway between Jesup and Brunswick.
A tornado (waterspout) was near the Sidney Lanier bridge. The spout moved slowy and became rain-wrapped while dissipating over nearby marshland.
The Jekyll Island Port Authority reported a few trees and power lines blown down near the campground on the island.
Daily rainfall total of 4.9 inches was measured on Fleming Island. Radar indicated 4.6 inches of storm total rainfall for the location.
Lifeguards reported 4 rip current rescues at Jacksonville Beach that day with numerous rip currents sighted along the beach.

A tin roof was partially torn off of a home located along State Road 32 near the railroad crossing between Ambrose and Douglas. The time of damage was estimated and based on radar. The cost of damage was estimated.

Severe flash flooding occurred in White Springs with roads washed out to a depth of 8 to 12 feet. The first roadway washed out was 1st Street which was completely severed. The water then flowed along a stream bed to Jewett Street which was also completely severed to a depth of 12 ft. One culvert pipe was completely washed away and was not located. Kendrick Street was then flooded and approximately 20 ft of road bed was either washed away or undermined. The cost of damage was estimated, and it is likely grossly under-estimated.
An observer measured 2.39 inches of rainfall in 45 minutes. Minor flooding was also reported.
Power lines were damaged along State Road 13 by thunderstorm wind gusts. The time of damage was based on radar.
Power lines were damaged along State Road 13 near Colee Cove. The time of damage was based on radar.
Power lines were damaged which caused power outages near Butler Beach. The time of damage was based on radar.
Power lines were damaged with widespread power outages near northern Palm Coast.
A substation at Highway 23 and Hinson Farm Road was struck by lightning. A power outage occurred which affected 1,577 customers. The cost of electrical damage was estimated.

At 7:30 am, the NWS employee reported flooding near Marsh Hammock Drive East. At 8:49 am, significant flooding was reported in areas near 10th Avenue South and 8th Avenue in Jacksonville Beach. Tropical storm force wind gusts started to impact Flagler County around 4 pm on Friday Nov. 26th. At 4:10 pm, a wind gust to 43 mph was measured in East Palm Coast. Friday evening, a measured gust of 48 mph was measured near Flagler Beach. At 12:05 pm on the 27th, spotters in Flagler Beach reported surf heights of 6 feet. There were no reports of any major erosion. The Flagler Beach Pier was closed on the 26th and the 27th. High astronomical tides combined with onshore flow did create flooding problems on the afternoon of Sunday the 28th, when, at 3 pm, very minor tidal flooding was reported on the Intracoastal Waterway south of Flagler Beach at South 26th Street and South Daytona Avenue. This area is normally flood prone during higher than normal tides, and there was no water threat to structures or roads.

St. Johns County Emergency Management reported coastal flooding around 7:05 pm on the evening of the 26th in St. Augustine. Water was going over the seawall south of the Bridge of Lions. Protective actions were taken. At 7:28 pm that evening, the St. Augustine AWOS station at the airport reported a gust of 49 mph. At 10 pm that evening, the St. Augustine C-Man station reported winds sustained at 36 mph with gusts to 48 mph. At 11 pm that evening, the St. Augustine C-Man reported measured sustained winds of 34 kts (39 mph) with a gust to 44 kts (51 mph).

A maximum tide level of 6.59 feet was observed at the Mayport Tide Gage. Shallow coastal flooding typically begins along the northeast Florida coast near Mayport when the tidal departure is near 6.4 ft MLLW.

Very minor tidal flooding was reported from the Intracoastal Waterway south of Flagler Beach. Water covered the road at South 26th Street and South Daytona Avenue. This area is normally flood prone during higher than normal tides. There was no threat to structures and the roads were not closed.

Widespread power outages and sporadic trees down occurred across the county over the 2 day period due to saturated grounds and gusty onshore flow with non-convective wind gusts up to 40 to 50 mph on May 3rd. On May 3rd, the county Park Department closed Princess Place Preserve as a precaution due to coastal flooding and the chance of trees falling due to saturated grounds.

Potato plants were severely damaged, and about 60% of the St. Johns County potato crop was likely lost. The cost of potato crop damage to about 8,500 acres of plants was estimated to be around $38,250,000, based on a yield of $4.5K/acre of potatoes. Melons and field corn crops were also damaged. The County Commission voted to pursue federal disaster relief funding. The crops were maintained through late season freezes in February and March, so many farmers were trying to rebound from these expensive events. The damage from the heavy rainfall and hail was very devastating to farmers and suppliers.

During the evening hours, between 655 pm and 710 pm EST on December 14, 2013, a tornado with maximum strength of EF1 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale touched down and crossed the northern sections of Palm Coast in Flagler County Florida. The tornado initially touched down north of Espanola on an intermittend track. The tornado then intensified to its maximum strength of 95 to 110 across the B section (Indian Trails and Pine Lakes neighborhoods) and western F sections of Palm Coast on a continuous path ranging in width from approximately 75 yards to a maximum of around 150 yards on Bannbury Lane. The tornado weakened as it moved northeast toward the coast with a path width of 25 to 50 yards across the eastern F section and Hammock area.  ||The location of the initial touchdown was near 29.52 degrees north latitude and 81.31 degrees west longitude. The location of the final damage was near 29.61 degrees north latitude and 81.19 degrees west longitude.  The total distance between the initial touchdown and final damage was approximately 9.5 miles with the longest continuous path approximately 1 mile in the B section of Palm Coast.  ||Media reported 7 homes were destroyed and more than 150 damaged when the tornado struck Palm Coast. Palm Coast city officials stated that 142 homes were partially damaged in the Indian Trails neighborhood and 22 homes had moderate damage. The damage was estimated at more than $5 million. No injuries were reported. The area was cluttered with downed trees and house debris.  The tornado downed power lines, blew out windows, knocked down trees and power poles and ripped away roof shingles.

A low-end EF1 tornado damaged 7 homes, downed power lines, and snapped trees. The tornado touched down about 8 miles north of Blackshear along Walkerville Road around 12:50 pm. Low end EF1 damage was noted along the tornado path as it crossed Georgia State Road 121/15. Including damage to 7 homes, power lines and large trees snapped.  EF0 damage was noted after the tornado crossed Georgia State Road 121/15, with the tornado lifting after an approximate 5.7 mile path near Spotted Farm Road and Songbird Place, or about 14 miles north of Blackshear. The tornado width varied from 60-100 yards.

The tornado touched down near Radio Station Road. High end EF1 damage occurred along the path east of Johnson Lake Road along Georgia State Road 32. In this path the tornado severely damaged two mobile homes including a double wide trailer in which the walls were separated, the frame bent and flipped on its side. Large trees were snapped along the path. EF0 damage was noted along most of the path as the tornado tracked from Radio Station Road to McCarty as the storm approached State Road 32. The tornado continued northeast and weakened as it cross Ten Mile Creek over Mallard Road with a track ceasing near Bobwhite Road. The width of the tornado ranged between 30-50 yards. Two injuries occurred with one mobile home, and one resident was life-flighted with critical injuries. Both victims survived. The tornado was an EF1 with maximum winds of 100-110 mph.

The tornado continued on an east to east-northeast path into the Palm Cay subdivision, where it reached its maximum intensity of EF1. Spotter EF0 damage was noted just south of SW 103rd Street at the conclusion of the tornado path, which was about 2 miles in length. The duration of this tornado was likely less than 5 minutes. The tornado moved ashore and pushed just south of Hendricks Elementary snapping trees and power lines. Several structures were impacted by falling trees and limbs. Initial damage was tightly clustered with a path of approximately 200 yards. As the tornado crossed Phillips Highway several businesses sustained roof damage. Trailers in the Pine Oaks mobile home park were damaged as well. The tornado began to track more southeast as it passed I-95 and widened to 350 yards as it neared Englewood High School. At about 5:58 pm, the tornado began to weaken and dissipate. A wide swath of straight line winds continued to cause damage farther to the south and east of the path until shortly after 6 pm. The path width varied from 200-350 yards along a 3.45 mile path. The tornado lasted 5-6 minutes with the maximum wind speeds reached 104 mph.

High astronomical tides were recorded at the NOS station at Mayport. At 8 pm local time on 9/26, the gage measured 3.77 ft NAVD88 datum. This was about 0.42 above the highest astronomical tide of 3.35 ft above NAVD88 datum. . At 9 pm the NOS tidal gage on the St. Johns River at the Dames Point Bridge reached 3.21 ft which was about 0.80 ft above the highest astronomical tide of 2.41 ft above NAVD88 datum. At 10 pm, the public reported via social media street flooding near Hogan's Creek in downtown Jacksonville on East Monroe Street due to high tide along the creek. At 8:24 am on 9/27 the NOS Station at Mayport reached 3.79 ft which was about 0.44 ft above the highest astronomical tide of 3.35 ft above NAVD88 datum. At 9:36 am the NOS tide gage on the St. Johns River at the Dames Point Bridge reached 3.23 ft which was about 0.82 ft above the highest astronomical tide of 2.41 ft above NAVD88. At 11 am on 9/28, Clarks Fish Camp in the Julington Creek had tidal flooding in the parking lot and inside the restaurant for the past 3-4 days. At 11 am on 9/30, significant beach erosion of 2-4 ft occurred along north portions of Atlantic Beach over the past few days. Tidal marks showed water reached the dune line at most locations.

On 9/26 at 8:45 pm the NOS tide gage in Fernandina Beach reported 4.96 ft above NAVD88 which was 0.58 ft above the highest astronomical tide of 4.38 ft NAVD88. At 8:54 am on 9/27, the NOS gage at Fernandina Beach reach 4.93 ft which was 0.55 ft above the highest astronomical tide of 4.38 ft NAVD88 datum.

At 8:15 pm on 9/26 the the USGS tide gage at the St. Simons Island Village Pier measured 5.25 ft above NAVD88 datum. This was 0.24 ft above the highest astronomical tide of 3.35 ft NAVD88. At 8:30 pm, the USGS tidal gage on the Brunswick River near the city of Brunswick measured 5.81 ft NAVD88. This was 0.21 ft above the highest astronomical tide of 5.6 ft NAVD88.

Apparent Rear Flank downdraft contacted ground. damage for about 1 mile downstream with a 100 yard wide swath. most debris laid out in straight line path with some lighter porch materials blown to the south. Likely the lighter materials were caught in an eddy. Trees and power lines downed, some roof damage with an open shed-garage area blown over.

Significant river flooding impacted residences along the St Johns River and Dunns Creek area. Some residences along Dunns Creek at water flood into their homes over 16 days, with the highest values at high tide. Some river front homes in the Sportsman Harbor subdivision had water rushing into their yards, over docks and over other outdoor property. This area is a known area at high risk for flooding (Cat 1 storm surge inundation zone and flood zone), and has repetitive losses due to river flood impacts. Putnam County EM reported that most flood impacts were considered minor during this high water period. ||In a report, Putnam County Emergency Management observed minor flooding in residential areas of the St. Johns River and Dunn���s Creek since October 5, 2015. No flooding affected habitability was reported to Putnam County Emergency Management. In accordance with Florida Division of Emergency Management and FEMA damage assessment guidance, all residential impacts were categorized as ���minimally affected.��� Most observed impacts were standing water in roadways, private driveways and public drainage systems.

At 9:12 am local time, the tide gage at Mayport measured a water level of 3.91 ft above NAVD88 datum. Minor coastal flooding typically begins at 3.8 ft. At 11 am local time, the tide gage at the Main Street Bridge in downtown Jacksonville measured a water level of 2.13 ft above NAVD88 datum. Minor coastal flooding typically begins at 2.0 ft.
The tide gage at Fernandina Beach measured at water level of 5.18 ft above NAVD88 datum. Minor coastal flooding typically begins at 4.8 ft.
The tide gage at the St. Simons Island Village Pier measured a water level of 5.72 ft above NAVD88 datum. Minor coastal flooding typically begins at 5.5 ft above NAVD88.
The tide gage at Sea Camp dock on Cumberland Island measured at water level of 5.59 ft above NAVD88 datum. Minor coastal flooding typically begins at 5.0 ft.

Clay County EM reported river flooding due to higher than normal water levels within the St. Johns River basin. Areas that were impacted were along Cedar Road along the SW bank of Doctor's Lake and Deer Island Road along the St. Johns River south of the Bayard Conservation Area near the mouth of Clarkes Creek.  In both areas, tidal flooding periodically closed road access to homes and properties.

Normally flood prone areas along the St. Johns River in San Marco and Southhampton experienced flooding of low lying areas during the high water period within the St. Johns River basin during early October 2015.

Widespread and significant flash flooding impacts occurred from Mayport southward to Neptune Beach during the evening hours with over 10 inches of rainfall measured at Naval Station Mayport for the day, but of which fell within 6 hours. The first report of flooding was reported around 7:26 pm by Fire Dept/Rescue with a road flooded just south of the Wonderwood Expressway. By 8:15 pm, the county emergency management  (EM) reported water flooded homes and apartments off of Mayport Road near the 2100 block. Around 9 pm, EM received multiple reports of roads flooded between 1st and 3rd Streets in Jacksonville Beach. EM also reported apartments were flooded between 2130 and 2160 Mayport Road, roads were flooded in Mayport Village along Broad Street and Ribault Street, numerous streets were closed in Neptune Beach due to flooding, and several residences along Forest Avenue, Oak Street and Magnolia Street has water within them. A vehicle drove into the ditch along the 100 block of Penman Road because the driver could not make out the edge of the road due to flooding. Also around 9 pm, EM relayed that flooding impacted all of Atlantic Beach with the worst hit areas including Aquatic Drive, Cavella Road, Skate Road, Selva Marina Drive and the north end of the city in the area of 19th Street and 20th Street. Many of these roads were completely inundated with water and water flowed into some residences along these streets. The police department responded to several calls for stranded vehicles due to flood water. At 9 pm, EM reported a few units at the Admirals Walk Apartment complex were affected by flood waters. Units at Mariners Village Apartments were also flooded. The Arium Apartments at 2160 Mayport Road at 32 units affected by flooding last night. The Red Cross set up a service center to assist affected residents. Six condos along Seminole Road had water flow inside. Around 10:12 pm, a spotter reported water across the Days Inn parking lot near Atlantic and Aquatic drive with about 3 ft of standing water in the lot. Cars were submerged in the parking lot. Water entered part of the hotel. Aquatic drive was closed due to flood water about 2 ft deep in some areas. At 10:41 am on Nov. 9th, EM reported Palm Avenue in Atlantic Beach was impassable due to flooding. The street runs into Howell Park which was under water. The creek near city hall along Seminole Road and Palm Avenue is still very high but has subsided some and the parking lot for city hall and Russell Park is not longer flooded. The cost of damage was unknown, and is likely an underestimate.

West of Stockton Street fresh water rainfall runoff was expected to be the primary cause of flooding. Kings Street was also flooded. Parts of McCoys Creek Blvd were closed due to flood waters. Minor damage occurred near Indian Mound Road and damage became more significant as the storm moved over the Manor-Millwood Road north. Damage to structures and trees was more signficant near Mullis Road where an old travel trailer was rolled and destroyed. A trailer in the area also had its rooof removed. Strong thunderstorms moved across the Ocala Regional Airport and produced a gust to 42 mph at 1:50 pm on June 6th. The peak wind at the airport occurred June 6th at 1750Z and was 36 kts from the SSW. Isolated tree damage was reported in squalls. Ground truth storm total rainfall ranged from 2.93 inches at 1 NNE Wiersdale to 6.11 inches at 4 N of Flemington.

Scattered tree and limb damage was reported due to gusty winds in squalls especially in the Oak Leaf, Fleming Island, Middleburg and Keystone Heights areas on Tue, 6/6, when a strong squall with wind gusts of 40-50 mph moved across the county. The south fork of Black Creek rose quickly from about 0.5 ft to a crest of near 13.8 ft due to a basin average rainfall of 4 to 6 inches within 24 hours of rainfall start. The site did not reach flood stage. The peak wind gust at Naval Air Station Jacksonville, just NE of Clay County was 36 kts from the SW on June 6th at 1927Z. The peak wind gust measured at Keystone Heights airport was 25 kts from the SW on June 6th at 0955Z. The peak wind gust at Red Bay Point (Shands Bridge) was from the SW of 31 kts on June 6th at 1924Z. Ground truth measured rainfall ranged from 7.10 inches 2 WSW of Picolata to 2.91 inches 1 NNE of Orange Park. Most locations measured 4-8 inches of rainfall across the southern tier of the county.

Impacts started in Duval County during the afternoon of the 6th just before 3:30 pm local time across the Jacksonville Westside when a squall line of storms produced a EF1 tornado near Normandy and Blair Road. The details of this damage will be in a separate Storm Data Tornado entry. As the Westside-Crystal Springs tornado dissipated, the thunderstorm rear-flank downdraft moved through a neighborhood northeast of the dissipating funnel cloud. The downdraft contacted the ground near West Beaver Street and moved northeast through the Watershed Drive,m Maple Avenue and Orme Road areas. The details of this downburst will also be in a separate Storm Data Event.  Numerous reports of trees blown included the following as the strong storms moved across the county, at 3:25 pm 5 W Normandy trees were blown down near Interstate 10 and Chaffee Road and at 3:25 pm trees were blown down near the intersection of Cathy Tripp Road and Old Plank Road.  At 3:50 pm, the peak wind gust at the Jacksonville International Airport ASOS was 43 mph. At 3:15 pm on the 6th, Cecil Field measured at peak wind gust of 25 kts from the south. Storm Total rainfall for the event ranged from 3.94 inches 4 ENE of Mandarin to 3.15 1 NW of Neptune Beach. Most rainfall across the inland portion of the county ranged from 2 to 4 inches, which included a measured 2.05 inches at the Jacksonville International Airport.

Impacts from T.S. Colin started after about 3:30 pm on June 6th as a squall line of strong storms moved east across the county. Scattered reports of trees and power lines were received as gusts of 43-50 mph occurred within this squall. At 3:30 pm, trees were blown down near Hogan's Creek. At 3:35 pm, three trees were uprooted at the intersection of Beach Blvd and St. John's Bluff Road, along with multiple large limbs down. At 3:40 pm, tree were reported down by a possible downburst near the Florida State College Jacksonville Southside campus. At 3:57 pm, a sensor at Huguenot Park reported a SW wind gust sustained at 51 mph with a gust to 63 mph. Other wind speed observations included a peak gust of 30 kt at Craig Airfield at 0311Z on the 7th, 37 kts at Mayport Naval Station on the 7th at 0359Z, and at Blount Island Command a gust of 40 kts was measured on the 6th at 1948Z. At 6 pm on June 6th, Mayport Village had wind gusts of at least 55 mph which caused some small limbs to come down. A power line was blown down at hte corner of Henry Road an Rebault Park. Over 4 inches of rainfall were measured at Mayport as of 6 pm on the 6th. At 10:45 pm on the 6th, a sensor at Jacksonville Beach pier measured a wind gust to 42 mph. Rainfall amounts across coastal Duval county generally ranged between 3 and 5 inches, including 4.37 inches about 1 NNW of Jacksonville Beach, 2 SW of San Pablo measured 3.26 inches and near 2.75 inches near Ortega.

Impacts from Colin began across Flagler county around 4 pm on the 6th. A wind gust of 41 mph was measured at 4:19 pm and another gust of 44 mph was measured at Marineland at 1:10 am on June 7th by a county owned weather station. Storm total rainfall near Marineland ranged from 3-5 inches. The Flagler County EOC measured a storm total rainfall of 4.61 inches since about 4 pm on June 6th. Several wall clouds were reported near Flagler Beach around 4:06 pm on June 6th through 5:20 pm. Storm total rainfall near Flagler Beach ranged from 2-4 inches. Storm total rainfall amounts across Palm Coast generally ranged from 3-6 inches within 24 hours. At 11:03 pm 7 W of Bunnell a tree was blown down across County Road 305 at County Road 302. At 2:55 am on June 7th, the AWOS stationat the Flagler County Airport measured a wind gust to 45 mph. Ground truth rainfall amounts ranged from 2.66 inches about 2 miles NNW of Flagler Beach to 5.07 inches about 1 mile WNW of Palm Coast.
At 3:30 pm on the 6th, trees were blown down along County Road 108 along Highway 1 in Hilliard. Minor tree damage occurred elsewhere in the county.

The county experienced isolated tree and power line damage due to wind gusts. Average rainfall ranged from 4 to 7 inches. The main impacts included flooded roads, especially east of Interstate 95. Two sink holes were reported, one at Colee Cover Branch Road and the second at Old Dixie and Venetian. A culvert washed out at Dan Manual Road. At 10:23 pm on June 6th, the St. Augustine airport AWOS measured at wind gust to 41 mph. At 11:31 pm, the C-man SAUF1 in St. Augustine measured a wind gust of 45 kt. Ground truth storm total rainfall included 6.93 inches about 2 miles NNW of Bakersville, 5.74 inches 1 mile W of St. Augustine Shores, 4.88 inches about 5 WSW of Durbin, and 4.71 inches at the St Augustine Airport.

The county had scattered reports of trees down due to wind gusts, especially across Gainesville and High Springs. There was one report of a tree down in Hawthorne. Minor damage occurred to a structure an several trees were blown down due to an unconfirmed tornado. Street flooding was reported in Gainesville and one apartment complex in Gainesville reported flooding in the complex entrance. The highest peak wind gust recorded at the Gainesville airport was 35 kts on the 6th at 1809Z. Storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 8.18 inches abuot 2 miles NNE of Micanopy to around 7.12 inches about 1 mile SE of Gainesville. Rainfall across the northern tier of the county ranged from 3.93 inches about 7 miles north of Newberry to 3.25 inches 3 miles NW of High Springs.
Possible tornado touchdown south of the UF Campus. Not confirmed. Minor damage occurred to a structure and several trees were blown down.

The tornado touched down near Normandy Blvd and Blair Road around 3:25 pm local time. Damage in this area was minor EF0 damage with some fencing blown down and trees damaged. The vortex continued along Blair Road maintaining the same intensity until it reached Wood Dove Way. From there to Interstate 10, EF1 damage was observed. The funnel then moved across the Publix Distribution Center flipping empty trucks and then NNE to Arbee Road. As the Westside-Crystal Springs tornado dissipated, the thunderstorm rear flank downdraft moved through a neighborhood northeast of the dissipating funnel. The tornado dissipated around 3:35 pm. The rear flank downdraft contacted the ground near West Beaver Street and moved northeast through the Watershed Drive, Maple Ave, and Orme Road areas. The predominant damage was to trees with some roof damage on Maple Street. There were reports of damage to residences, businesses, and trees along the tornado path. Some homes had parts of roofs partially torn off or damaged. Maximum wind speed 100 mph.

Wind damage was reported on State Road 100 near Keystone Heights were about 20 large oak trees were blown down. Two of these trees blocked driveways and one fell onto an unoccupied trailer. School buses were held Monday afternoon due to a tornado warning in effect as a strong squall line moved across the county. Measured storm total rainfall amounts included 3.85 inches about 3 miles east of Starke.

As the Westside-Crystal Springs Tornado was dissipating the thunderstorm rear-flank downdraft moved across a neighborhood northeast of the dissipating funnel. The downdraft contacted the ground near West Beaver Street and moved northeast through the Watershed Drive, Maple Ave., and Orme Road areas. The path length was about 1 to 1.5 miles in length and about .1 mile wide. The prominent damage was to trees and some roof damage on Maple Street.

As the Westside-Crystal Springs Tornado was dissipating the thunderstorm rear-flank downdraft moved across a neighborhood northeast of the dissipating funnel. The downdraft contacted the ground near West Beaver Street and moved northeast through the Watershed Drive, Maple Ave., and Orme Road areas. The path length was about 1 to 1.5 miles in length and about .1 mile wide. The prominent damage was to trees and some roof damage on Maple Street.

The main impacts across the county were due to heavy rainfall and gusty winds in squalls. County average storm total rainfall amounts were 4-7 inches with isolated higher amounts near Bostwick. Several power lines were damaged and several trees or tree limbs were blown down which blocked roads across the county. Some ground truth storm total rainfall amounts included 6.17 inches about 3 miles north of Georgetown, 5.13 inches about 5 miles south of Putnam Hall, and 4.76 inches about 1 mile NW of Georgetown. About 4 miles SE of Crescent City 3.57 inches was measured.

Scattered wind damage was reported across the county. It included 5 reports of trees blown down across roads, 1 report of a tree on a power line, 1 report of a tree on a vehicle, 1 report of a tree on a shed, and 5 reports of sparking power lines. Storm total rainfall amounts included 3.86 inches measured about 1 mile SW of St. Simons Island, 2.55 inches at the St. Simons Malcom McKinnon Airport, and 2.13 inches 3 miles south of Boys Estate. The peak wind gust measured at the Brunswick Glynco Airport was 25 kts on the 6th at 5:35 pm.

Lightning caused 7 new fires in the Osceola National Forest on Sunday afternoon that burned 112 acres. Recent rainfall helped contain fire activity. By August 2nd, 100% of the fire was contained.

A 45 year old female died while trying to save her 11 year old son at the north end of Huguenot Park about a quarter mile from Ft. George Inlet. The drowning was attributed to both tidal currents and rip currents. Huguenot Park Beach has stronger ocean currents compared to other nearby beaches per Beach Patrol and Duval County EM. The park is on an island where Ft. George Inland borders to the north and the Mayport jetties border to the south. Changes also occurred to bathymetry in the area with sand bars and steeper drop offs into the ocean.

Alachua county had numerous trees and power lines blown down and a few trees snapped off mid-section. Several homes were damaged by fallen trees and large limbs within Gainesville city limits. Around 1:30 am on Sept. 2nd, a couple of trees were reported down in Gainesville and also on the University of Florida campus. At 2:07 am, a wind gust of 44 mph was measured at the Gainesville Regional airport. At 2:30 am, emergency management reported 36 trees down in the county with 5 homes damaged. At 3:38 am, the ASOS station at the Gainesville Regional airport reported a peak storm wind gust of 51 mph from the south. A location 3 miles SW of High Springs measured a storm total rainfall of 4.53 inches and the Gainesville Regional Airport measured 4.42 inches (1200 UTC Sep 1 through 1200 UTC Sep 3).

Storm total rainfall measured 1 mile west of Glen St. Mary was 4.31 inches. A RAWS weather station called Eddy Tower in the Olustee National Forest measured a peak wind gust of 30 mph on Sept. 2nd at 4:04 am and the RAWS weather station Olustee measured a peak wind gust of 43 mph on Sept. 1st at 10:04 pm.
Scattered trees and power lines were blown down across the county. Storm total rainfall amounts ranged from 3.21 inches 1 mile ESE of Starke to 3.01 inches 2 miles NE New River.

At 2 am on Sept. 2nd, one male died when a tree fell on his tent in a  homeless cap behind the Diamond Oil Company along Southeast Lake Weir Avenue. Scattered trees were reported blown down across the county. At 4 am on Sept. 2nd, a large tree was blown down along SE 39th Street in Ocala which impacted 2 residences. A home was damaged when a tree fell on it. A tree was blown down on a roadway, and a vehicle struck the fallen tree. Two people in the vehicle were transported to the hospital. Storm total rainfall included 2.42 inches measured 2 miles NW of Belleview and 3.27 inches 2 miles W of McIntosh. The peak wind gust measured at the Ocala International Airport was 45 mph measured on Sept. 2nd at 4:15 am. The RAWs weather station at Lake Georgia in the Ocala National Forest measured a peak wind gusts of 35 mph on Sept. 2nd at 10:04 am.

At 11:45 pm on Sept 1st, a social media report indicated a tree was blown down onto a car at Highway 47 south of Lake City. Minor injuries were reported. At 2:15 am on Sept. 2nd, a wind gust of 43 mph was measured at the Lake City Gateway Airport. Storm total rainfall amounts of 5.77 inches were measured at Oleno State Park. Two miles ENE of the city of Columbia, 3.64 inches were measured.

Rainfall totals ranged from 4 to 6 inches across the county with estimated sustained winds of 40 to 45 mph. Downed trees damaged one home and one vehicle. At 1:30 am on Sept. 2nd, about 20 trees were reported blown down. Ground truth storm total rainfall included 4.22 inches 3 miles N of Bell and 4.33 inches 6 miles WNW of Newberry.

Trees and power lines were blown down county-wide. Emergency services in the county were discontinued due to the large number of trees down. The speed sensor at the Hamilton County Emergency Operations Center failed during the event. An estimated 3K customers were without power. At 3 am on Sept. 2nd, several trees were blown down in Jasper. Ground truth storm total rainfall included 3.40 inches 1 mile ENE of Jasper.

Peak wind gusts included 46 mph at 9:21 am at Craig Airfield in Arlington; 51 mph at Naval Station Mayport at 8:02 am on Sept. 2nd; 41 mph at the Terminal Channel Downtown Jacksonville at 11:25 pm Sept 1st; 51 mph at Buck Island at 9:18 am on Sept 2nd; 52 mph at Huguenot Park at 6:58 am on Sept. 2nd; and 53 mph at the WeatherFlow sensor located at Jacksonville Beach Pier at 10:19 am on Sept. 2nd. The peak wind measured at the NOS Station in Mayport was 48 mph on Sept. 2nd at 12:42 pm and at Blount Island Command NOAA Ports 48 mph on Sept. 2nd at 8:12 am. Maximum storm surge values included 0.86 ft (3.02 ft) at Mayport and 1.00 ft at the Dames Point bridge (tide 2.22 ft).

Multiple roads were closed in St. Augustine including West San Carlos, Valencia Street and parts of King Street. Most streets were opened by 1115 am later that morning. One home on Viscaya Blvd and two homes on Shore Blvd had minor flooding inside. The cost of damage was unknown.

Extensive flooding of Fletcher Avenue occurred, especially near the 600 block section which extended southward to the 1500 block section of Fletcher Avenue and Southward to Ocean Drive. These areas are just east of Egan's Creek. Water level observations indicated a potential seiche flooding trialing the storm surge that likely flooded Egan's Creek as Hurricane Matthew started to track farther North of the local area. As winds shifted to the NNW, surge water was pushed back across the Edgan's Creek Drainage which funneled southward and caused flooding.

The tornado started in extreme western Appling County, possibly extreme SE Jeff Davis county and tracked NE at 50-60 mph before lifting along the NW part of the town of Baxley. The event occurred mainly along or parallel to Zoar Road.  The peak wind was near 110 mph in the vicinity of County Farm Road. The most significant damage was in the area near Zoar Methodist Church where structural damage occurred to the church including roof damage and tilting the steeple and other outbuildings in the area. Extensive tree damage occurred to both hard and softwood trees with trees uprooted, snapped and large limbs twisted.

This tornado begin in northern Atkinson county and tracked NE around 50 mph across southern Coffee county before it lifted near Mora Road. As the tornado moved across Coffee, it produced EF1 damage with peak winds near 110 mph. The tornado crossed the Atkinson/Coffee county line across Brawns Johnson Road near a residence within the 400 block. Extensive tree damage including snapped and leveled pine trees and some damage to hard woods was observed along the tornado track including along Talmadge McKinnon Road, Brawns Johnson Road and along portions of the Mora Highway between County Roads 48 and 30 where four chicken houses were damaged, including two completely destroyed. There was also additional extensive property damage to agricultural structures occurred along this path.

The tornado started in extreme northern Atkinson County and continued to track NE at 50 mph crossing over into Coffee County and lifting near the Mora Highway where the most damage occurred. The tornado tracked NE for about 1.6 miles in Atkinson County where it produced EF1 damage along Ice Plant Road to trees. As Ice Plant Road merged into Talmadge McKinnon Road in Atkinson county, there were a couple of outbuildings that were demolished and debris blown into a pine stand which was also heavily damaged. A residence at this intersection had extensive tree damage, including one pine tree that impaled a vehicle. Numerous agricultural structures including silos and elevated irrigation systems where lofted and carried across pastures along Talmadge McKinnon Road northward toward the Coffee County Line.

An extensive wind damage event occurred across Clay county associated with several long tracked severe downbursts. One downburst was the rear-flank downdraft of a tornadic supercell that produced an EF1 tornado in Lawtey, just west of the western Clay county line. As the RFD descended, a severe downburst raced across the northern tier o Clay county from about 10:08 pm local time through 10:35 pm local time which caused widespread wind damage to structures in Middleburg, Doctor's Inlet, Doctor's Lake, Fleming Island, and Orange Park. Another storm within the squall line impacted Keystone Heights where a wind gust of 50 mph was measured at 10:15 pm by the AWOS at the Keystone Airport. Peak wind gusts were estimated between 70-80 mph per Storm Surveys. Below is a timeline of wind damage reports across Clay county as reported to the NWS for this wind event. ||At 10:08 pm, Emergency Management reported multiple homes with trees down on them near Keystone Heights. At 10:15 pm, the general public reported numerous trees and power lines were blown down along State Road 100 and Twin Lakes Road, about 2 miles SE of Keystone Heights. There was also a report of a roof blown off of a home. Also around 10:15 pm, a NWS storm spotter about 6 miles NNE of Middleburg reported a large live oak tree was blown down and a small gazebo was destroyed. There was also small hail observed, but size was not reported. At 10:15, the public reported tree tops were snapped and damage near Asbury Lake with small hail (unknown size). At 10:20 pm, a HAM radio operator located 3 miles NE of Lakeside reported a tree was blown down and partially blocked Doctor's Lake Drive in Orange Park. A storm survey of this area later revealed extensive large tree damage and structural damage to homes, some uninhabitable due to the extent of damage. Many trees were over 1 ft in diameter, which included large live oaks and water oaks. Around this time, a spotter later relayed fence damage, a flag pole blown down and tree limb damage in Lakeside with wind gusts estimated at 70 mph. At 10:20 pm, a HAM radio operator about 5 miles SE of Lakeside reported another large tree was blown down which partially blocked the Woodlands Subdivision on Fleming Island. Around the same time, a large pine tree was reported blown down by the media along Cornell Road in Middleburg. Around this time, a spotter in Middleburg estimated 60 mph wind gusts. This tree damaged power lines. Another report from the media around this time indicated a tree was blown down on a home along Main Street about 3 miles ENE of Middleburg. At 10:25 pm, the media reported extensive tree down, fence damage, and patio furniture debris at the intersection of Kingsley Avenue and Doctor's Lake Drive in Orange Park Florida. At this same time, a NWS employee was driving into work along Highway 17 between Pace Island on Fleming Island and the Doctor's Lake Bridge. The employee experienced very strong westerly wind gusts of 60-70 mph. At 10:25 pm, the public reported tops of trees blown down and hail of unknown size about 6 miles SW of Lakeside. At 10:27 pm, tree damage was reported in Orange Park along U.S. Highway 17 between Stowe and Milwaukee Avenues.||There was one injury reported in Clay county with this event. A shelter was opened for residents. Extensive damage to homes occurred in Keystone Heights, Clay Hill and Orange Park. This tornado may have initiated as a water spout that moved onshore at Vilano Beach. Minimal damage was reported in Vilano Beach with greater tree damage discovered west of Vilano Beach where a few trees were snapped and uprooted. The tornado then crossed Highway 1 and caused additional tree and roof damage from 4th Street toward Porter Road before dissipating in the 12 Mile Swamp Conservation Area. Radar indicated a tornado debris signature. This tornado had peak winds of 85-100 mph.

This tornado touchdown in northern Flagler county just south of Marineland. Damage was limited to trees. Structural damage was not reported. A tornado debris signature was detected along the path. The tornado remained over the Pellicer Creek Conservation Area before dissipating just west of Interstate 95.

This tornado passed the northern side of Castillo de San Marcos and uprooted 2 trees before strengthening to EF1 and moving toward Huguenot Cemetery. Multiple trees were uprooted and snapped in the cemetery. The tornado continued moving west in the vicinity of Orange Street before dissipating just before reaching Highway 1. This tornado likely began as a water spout offshore.

events.event_narrative: A tornado, which was spanned by the same from mesocyclone which moved through Lake City earlier in the day, moved through northeastern Baker County. One brick residence was completely destroyed at 11456 O. C. Horne Road, in Sanderson and a second residence at 20192 Golden Grass Farms Road had tin roof blown. The tornado continued toward the St Marys River but lifted prior to reaching the river. An additional touchdown occurred in Charlton County, Georgia.

A total of 5 houses were damaged with one house sustaining major structural damage. Possible tornado induced damage was along State Road 185 near Mile Marker 2. Numerous power lines were reported down in southern Charlton County. The mesocyclone which dropped this tornado was tracked through Columbia and Baker Counties in Florida and spanned several tornadoes there. The mesocyclone also moved into western Nassau County Florida with a brief touchdown there.
Minor damage to outhouse and trees knocked down along River Road.

National Weather Service Storm Survey of the tornado track indicated most damage was EF1 scale with a small area of EF2 damage near NE Denver Street opposite a large field. Numerous Trees and power lines were snapped or blown over by the storm.  Truck and trailers were also blown over in an industrial park. Nineteen homes were destroyed, twenty-one suffered major damage, and twenty had minor damage.  Two businesses were destroyed with six suffering major damage.  One female fatality occurred when a tree went through her mobile home. A male indirect fatality occurred when trying to connect a power generator. The mesocyclone which spanned this tornado was tracked across Taylor, Lafayette, and Suwannee Counties prior to this touchdown and it later spanned tornadoes in Baker, Charlton and Nassau Counties.

Emergency Management received reports of trees down and an old shed blow into the trees off County Road 137. This report was received by emergency management at 1002 a.m. EST. The mesocyclone which spawned this tornado was tracked through Taylor and Lafayette counties and later spanned tornadoes in Columbia, Baker, Charlton, and Nassau counties.

The mesocyclone which spawned this tornado was tracked across north Florida and southeast Georgia from Taylor County through Lake City to near Cumberland Island.

The Mayport, Florida tide gauge had measured low tide of -2.57 feet Mean Lower Low Water which was about 1.67 feet below predicted tide of -0.90 feet around 1930Z. Previous record was -2.28 feet Mean Lower Low Water on 2/18/1996.

Fernandina Beach, Florida tide gauge measured -3.12 feet Mean Lower Low Water which was about 2.45 feet below predicted tide of -0.70 feet around 1942Z. Although not a record, this was roughly a foot from the record of -4.1 feet Mean Lower Low Water in 1940.

The St Simons Island, Georgia tide gauge measured a low tide of -3.31 feet Mean Lower Low Water which was about 2.36 feet below predicted tide of -0.95 feet around 2000Z. This appear to break the previous record of -2.39 feet Mean Lower Low Water in January 2001.

Minor wind damage was observed across the county, which included numerous trees blown down and power outages. At 730 pm on 10/10, a power lines was blown down near Haley Circle. Between 1025 pm and 11 pm on 10/10, numerous reports of wind damage were reported. At 1025 pm, a reported of damage to the roof of a convenience store was received. After a storm survey, it was confirmed that ta back office behind the store had its roof blown off, and it was laid onto the roof of the store.  At 10:25 pm, a report of a fallen tree onto a trailer was received in Bushnell. At 10:30 pm, a chicken house was blown down in Pridgen. There were unconfirmed reports of major roof damage to a church in Ambrose, but the church could not be found during the post storm survey. There were over 200 residents sheltered from mobile homes in the county.
A peak tropical storm force wind gust of 46 mph was measured at the Homverville Airport at 8:15 pm on 10/10. The county experienced widespread power outages and trees blown down or snapped.

Tropical storm force wind gusts impacted the county. At 10:25 pm on 10/10, the ASOS station at the Bacon County Airport measured a wind gust of 43 mph. On 10/11 at 12:50 am, the ASOS station measured a wind gust of 51 mph. This set a new record as the strongest wind gust reported at Alma during the month of October since records began in 1973.

National Weather Service Jacksonville Storm survey|revealed damage consistent with EF-1 tornado damage in Royal Drive|Subdivision east of I-95 and south of Jekyll Island Causeway in|Glynn County. A combination of waterspout and tornado likely|formed near I-95 on a section of the Little Satilla River before |causing damage within the subdivision. A couple dozen trees were |damaged with several snapped at the trunk. A Doppler Radar debris |signature was evident between 3-5,000 feet indicating lofted |tornado debris. The tornado damage concludes on the south side of|the Jekyll Island Causeway. The survey team was unable to find|damage west of I-95 so the start point given is where damage to |trees and docks began, however, it is possible that the tornado |started on the Little Satilla River farther west.

National Weather Service Jacksonville Storm Survey|revealed  damage consistent with EF-3 tornado damage at Naval |Submarine Base Kings Bay, which was confirmed by a 125 knot / 144 |mph maximum wind gust measurement from a docked Coast Guard |vessel. This is the strongest tornado in recent memory within the |National Weather Service Jacksonville's area of responsibility in |southeast Georgia, northeast and north central Florida. Four |injuries were reported by officials at Naval Submarine Base Kings |Bay. The tornado continued on an east-northeast path across |Cumberland Island, beginning from Old House Creek and exiting into|the Atlantic waters just south of the Stafford Beach Campground. |The tornado path across Cumberland Island was estimated by |Cumberland Island National Seashore park rangers to be |approximately one-third to one half mile wide. Significant tree |damage occurred within the tornado path across Cumberland Island, |with no structural damage reported. The main park road and several|trails on Cumberland Island were left impassable by the tree |damage.

The Compartment #1 fire was started by a lightning strike on Saturday May 18th.  The fire quickly increased in intensity around 2 pm on Sunday May 19th due to hot and dry conditions. By May 23rd, the fire was 98% contained and grew to 185 acres. There were not reports of property damage as the fire was held in the Okefenokee NWR.  On 6/6, the fire was 100% contained.

Two wildfires started along U.S. Highway 17 near the Nassau River off of Yellow Bluff Road. On May 22 around 345 pm, one fire was 100% contained with only 25% on the larger southernmost fire which was estimated at 150 acres just north of Yellow Bluff Road. The Yellow Bluff fire spread northwest and portions of Interstate 95 between Interstate 95 near mile marker 368. The right northbound lane of I-95 was closed due to the proximity of the wildfire. At 3:28 pm on 5/23, the Yellow Bluff fire was about 400 acres. Both lanes of I-95 were closed between mile markers 366 and 373 due to the proximity of the fire and smoke blowing over the interstate. The fire did spot on the west side of I-95 Florida Highway Partrol. Around 213 pm on 5/24, the fire was up to 600 acres in size and was about 30% contained. All lanes of Interstate 95 were re-opened except of the right northbound lane for fire emergency vehicle staging. Around 7:30 pm on 5/29, the fire was about 80% contained and was about 604 acres and holding with minimal smoke impacts to Interstate 95.

Emergency management and broadcast media reported flash flooding in downtown Jacksonville. At 4:52 pm, the media relayed photos on social media of water pooling inside the parking garage of a local business. The time of this rainfall flooding was on radar. At 5:10 pm, emergency management reported flooding outside of the McCoys Creek basin in downtown Jacksonville. There was not structure flooding at the time, with radar estimates of 2-3 inches/hour in this area. At 5:20 pm, local media reported flooding over Stockton Street in downtown Jacksonville with a video of vehicles driving through 1-1.5 of flood water submerging car tires and wheel wells. At 5:25 pm, Jacksonville Fire Rescue was responding to flood water entering the Jacksonville Downtown Public Library. The Libaray was closed due to water in the building. At 5:25 pm, media relayed a social media report of fire rescue on scene at the intersection of Market and Orange Streets in Jacksonville due to flood waters. This location was within the Hogan's Creek River Basin which is susceptible to flash floods.
